dialogue.scene: Omar and his sister Reem are talking about a new football video game at home.

p1.t: Omar, that's three hours on that game! What do you think about your screen time today?
To be honest, it's a bit too much. But this new football game is really addictive.
In my opinion, three hours is a waste of time. It's a beautiful day outside.
Maybe, but it isn't a complete waste. I'm learning to work with my team online.

p2.t: That's interesting. What do you think about playing real football instead?
Well, I think real football is better for my health, because I actually move.
Exactly. So let's go to the park after Asr. Dad can take us.
Fine! I'll save the game and come with you.

dialogue.focus: I think real football is better for my health, because I actually move.
qs: Why does Reem think three hours of gaming is a waste of time?
What does Omar think about real football?

speakout.scene: A gaming channel for kids is asking its viewers: should children have a daily screen-time limit? I'm the host, and I want to interview you.

prompts.q: What do you think about having a daily screen-time limit?

prompts.q: Which games or apps are a waste of time, in your opinion?

In your opinion, what is a good screen-time rule for families?

0-0.exit: Give me your opinion about video games in two sentences, and use 'because' in one of them.

dialogue.scene: Noura and her classmate Sara are in the school canteen at break time.

p1.t: Noura, what's your opinion of the new canteen menu?
Personally, I'm not keen on it. The pasta was tasteless yesterday.
Really? I liked the chicken wrap. I believe it's a healthy option too.
Maybe, but they stopped selling samosas! That's a real shame.

p2.t: In my opinion, it's good that they sell less fried food.
I suppose so. But I believe students should be able to choose.
What do you think about writing to the head teacher about it?
That's a great idea! Let's ask her to add fresh juice and dates.

dialogue.focus: I believe students should be able to choose.
qs: Why isn't Noura keen on the new menu?
What do the girls want to ask the head teacher to add?

prompts.q: What's your opinion of the food in our canteen?

prompts.q: Do you believe we should stop selling sweets and fizzy drinks?

qs: What do you think about students serving lunch, like in Japan?
In your opinion, should schools give free lunch to every student?

0-1.exit: Tell me your opinion of your school food in two sentences. Start one of them with 'Personally'.

dialogue.scene: Faisal and his cousin Sam have just watched an animated film at a cinema in Jeddah.

p1.t: So, Faisal, what did you think of the film?
I found it really funny, but the plot was a bit confusing in the middle.
Really? I thought the plot was clever. The ending surprised me.
True, the ending was great. But was the first film better?

p2.t: To be honest, I think the first one is a bit overrated. This one was better.
I'm not sure. How do you feel about films with so many songs?
I usually skip the songs at home! But overall, it was worth watching.
In my opinion, it's the best film this year. Let's tell the whole family tonight!

dialogue.focus: I found it really funny, but the plot was a bit confusing in the middle.
qs: What did Faisal find confusing?
What does Sam think about the first film?

dialogue.scene: Khalid and his friend Daniel, who lives in Riyadh, are watching Al-Hilal play Al-Nassr on TV.

p1.t: That was never a penalty! The referee made a terrible mistake.
If you ask me, it was a penalty. The defender pushed him.
Well, it seems unfair. Al-Nassr played much better in the first half.
Maybe, but they missed so many chances.

p2.t: So who do you think will win the league this year?
The way I see it, Al-Hilal has the strongest team, so they deserve to win.
I'm not sure. In my opinion, the league is very close this season.
We'll see! Quick, the second half is starting.

dialogue.scene: Reem lives in Riyadh. Her friend Lama lives in a small town in Qassim. They are talking on a video call.

p1.t: Lama, what do you think about living in a small town?
I love it. It's peaceful, and my grandparents live next door.
It seems to me that small towns are a bit boring. In Riyadh there's a lot to do.
That's true, but Riyadh is so crowded. How long does it take you to get to your swimming club?

p2.t: About forty minutes, because of the traffic jams every afternoon.
Forty minutes! I walk to my club in five.
OK, you win! But we have Riyadh Season, the Boulevard and huge malls.
I'm not sure, but I think a small town is still better for me. I'll visit you in winter, though!

dialogue.focus: It seems to me that small towns are a bit boring.

dialogue.scene: Students are recording a show for the school radio. Today's question is: 'Should students get homework every day?' Sultan is the presenter, and Majed is his guest.

p1.t: Welcome to School Radio! Should we get homework every day? Majed, what's your view on this?
From my point of view, a little homework every day makes sense. It helps us remember the lesson.
But many students say it's a waste of time. What do you think about that?
To be honest, some homework is boring. But the main reason we need it is practice.

p2.t: Some parents say their children feel too much pressure. Is that true?
Sometimes, yes, especially before exams. If you ask me, twenty minutes a day is enough.
Interesting! So you're not against homework?
No. I'm convinced that short homework is better than no homework at all.

dialogue.focus: From my point of view, a little homework every day makes sense.
qs: Why does Majed think homework makes sense?
How much homework is enough, in Majed's opinion?

speakout.scene: You're a guest on the school radio show, and I'm the presenter. Today's question is: 'Should students be allowed to bring phones to school?' Give your opinions with reasons, and ask for mine too.

dialogue.scene: Faisal and Omar are choosing what to eat at a food court in a mall in Dammam.

p1.t: I'm in the mood for kabsa. I love the chicken kabsa here.
So do I! It's the best kabsa in Dammam.
But I don't like it when the sauce is too spicy.
Neither do I. Last time my mouth was on fire!

p2.t: What about dessert? I really like kunafa.
Really? I don't. It's too sweet for me. I prefer ice cream.
I can't believe it! Everyone likes kunafa.
Well, it's just a matter of taste. My sister feels the same way.
OK, fair enough. Let's order the kabsa and decide on dessert later.

dialogue.focus: So do I! It's the best kabsa in Dammam.

I'm not keen on that. I can't sleep well in a tent.

dialogue.scene: Reem and her friend Emma have been learning to bake cakes from online videos. Emma loves it, but Reem isn't sure.

p1.t: I love learning to bake from online videos. I can watch them in my pyjamas!
Ha! I see your point, but I couldn't concentrate at all.
Why not? Your kitchen is so quiet.
Not when my little brothers are at home! They were a big distraction.

p2.t: OK, you've got a point. But the videos are free, and we don't waste time in traffic.
That's true, but my cake was a disaster. I prefer learning face to face with a real chef.
To be honest, I feel the same way. My cake looked like a pancake!
So let's try the baking workshop at the mall, and watch videos at home too.

dialogue.focus: I see your point, but I couldn't concentrate at all.
qs: Why couldn't Reem concentrate at home?

Maybe the phone. It's a camera, a map and a computer at the same time.
True! But I'd say the air conditioner. Life in Riyadh in summer is impossible without it!

dialogue.focus: It's a robot which cleans solar panels in the desert.
qs: What does the robot do?
What is the helmet used for?

speakout.scene: You've invented a new gadget for kids. I'm a judge on a TV show for young inventors. Describe your invention to me in detail.

prompts.q: What's your invention?
prompts.hint: Say 'It's a gadget which / that …'.

prompts.q: What is it used for?
prompts.hint: Use 'It's used for …ing' and give an example.

prompts.q: When will it come in handy?
prompts.hint: Describe a situation and say who it will help.

culture.title: Inventions from the Arab World
points: Al-Jazari, a famous inventor from about 800 years ago, designed amazing water clocks and machines.
The Arab scientist Ibn al-Haytham did important work on light and how our eyes see.
Today, Saudi universities like KAUST work on inventions for clean water and energy.
qs: Which invention do you think changed the world the most?
What gadget would you like someone to invent?

3-1.exit: Describe your favourite gadget in two sentences. Use 'which' or 'that' at least once.

3-2.objective: Today you will describe interesting places in detail using 'where'.
3-2.warmup: What's the most beautiful place you've ever visited?

expressions.def: important in history
expressions.frame: ___ is a historic place in my country.

expressions.def: to be known by many people for something
expressions.frame: My city is famous for ___.

expressions.def: very beautiful or exciting
expressions.frame: The view from ___ is breathtaking.

expressions.def: very, very old
expressions.frame: I'd love to see the ancient ___ in ___.

expressions.def: to be good enough that you should go there
expressions.frame: ___ is really worth a visit.

expressions.def: a person who travels to visit places for fun
expressions.frame: Lots of tourists visit ___ every year.

dialogue.scene: Omar has just come back from a family trip to AlUla. He shows some photos to his friend Sam.

p1.t: Where are these photos from, Omar?
AlUla! This is Hegra, the place where the Nabataeans built huge tombs in the rocks.
Wow, it looks ancient! How old is it?
About two thousand years old. It's a historic site, and it's famous for those tombs.

p2.t: And what's this? It looks like an elephant!
That's Elephant Rock, the place where we watched the sunset. The view was breathtaking.
Are there many tourists there?
Yes, lots, especially in winter. If you ask me, AlUla is really worth a visit.

dialogue.focus: This is Hegra, the place where the Nabataeans built huge tombs in the rocks.
qs: What is Hegra famous for?
What did Omar's family do at Elephant Rock?

speakout.scene: I'm a tourist visiting Saudi Arabia for the first time. I'm asking you, a local, about places to visit.

prompts.q: Which place in Saudi Arabia is really worth a visit?
prompts.hint: Name it and describe it with 'It's a place where …'.

prompts.q: What is your city or town famous for?
prompts.hint: Give two things and add details with 'where' or 'which'.

prompts.q: Where's the best place to watch the sunset?
prompts.hint: Describe it with adjectives like breathtaking or peaceful.

culture.title: UNESCO Sites in Saudi Arabia
points: In 2008, Hegra became the first place in Saudi Arabia on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
At-Turaif in Diriyah is the place where the first Saudi state began.
Al-Ahsa Oasis, where there are millions of palm trees, is also on the list.
qs: Which of these places would you like to visit? Why?
Why do you think it's important to protect historic places?

3-2.exit: Describe a place you love in two sentences. Use 'where' in one of them.

3-3.objective: Today you will describe people in your family using 'whose' and other details.
3-3.warmup: Who do you look like in your family?

expressions.def: to know who someone is because you have seen them before
expressions.frame: I didn't recognise ___ at first.

expressions.def: to look or act like an older person in your family
expressions.frame: I take after my ___ because we both ___.

expressions.def: to look the same as each other
expressions.frame: ___ and ___ look alike.

expressions.def: a funny or friendly name that people call you
expressions.frame: My nickname is ___ because ___.

expressions.def: having lots of curls
expressions.frame: The person in my family with curly hair is ___.

expressions.def: being the person who controls or looks after something
expressions.frame: In my house, ___ is in charge of ___.

dialogue.scene: Faisal is showing his friend Daniel an old family photo at his grandfather's house.

p1.t: Who are all these people, Faisal?
My family, twenty years ago! That's my grandfather, the man whose camel won a race.
Ha! And who's the boy with curly hair? I don't recognise him.
That's my dad! He was ten. People say I take after him.

p2.t: You really look alike! And who are the two boys whose shirts are the same?
Twins! My uncles Fahad and Faris. Their nickname was 'Copy and Paste'.
That's funny! Who's the man in charge of the barbecue?
My great-uncle Saad. He's the one whose stories everyone loves.

dialogue.focus: That's my grandfather, the man whose camel won a race.
qs: Why doesn't Daniel recognise the boy with curly hair?
What was the twins' nickname?

speakout.scene: Let's play a guessing game. Think of someone in your family or a famous person. Describe them using 'whose', 'who' and other details, and I'll guess.

prompts.q: Tell me about the person's family or the things they own.
prompts.hint: Use 'It's someone whose …' (for example, whose brother is a pilot).

prompts.q: Who do they take after in their family?
prompts.hint: Say who they look like or act like.

prompts.q: Do they have a nickname?
prompts.hint: Say the nickname and explain where it comes from.

culture.title: Names Around the World
points: In Saudi Arabia, many fathers are called 'Abu' + their oldest son's name, like Abu Fahad.
In Iceland, many family names are the father's first name + 'son' or 'dóttir'.
In China, the family name comes first and the given name comes second.
qs: Do you have a nickname? Who gave it to you?
Who in your family do you take after?

3-3.exit: Describe two people you know in two sentences. Use 'whose' in both of them.

3-4.objective: Today you will describe a lost thing and the place where you lost it in detail.
3-4.warmup: Have you ever lost something important?

expressions.def: to forget to take something with you
expressions.frame: I once left my ___ behind at ___.

expressions.def: used to say what material something is
expressions.frame: My ___ is made of ___.

expressions.def: completely new
expressions.frame: My ___ is brand-new.

expressions.def: a design of lines, shapes or colours
expressions.frame: My favourite ___ has a pattern of ___.

expressions.def: to be owned by someone
expressions.frame: This ___ belongs to ___.

expressions.def: a place where people take things that others have lost
expressions.frame: If I lose my ___, I'll ask at the lost and found.

dialogue.scene: Ali left his backpack on the metro in Riyadh. He is at the lost and found office, talking to an officer, Mr Nasser.

p1.t: Good morning. Welcome to the lost and found. How can I help you?
I left my backpack behind on the metro this morning. It was on the train which left Olaya at eight.
OK. Can you describe it?
It's a brand-new blue backpack which has a pattern of white stars. It's made of soft material.

p2.t: What was inside it?
My football boots and a lunch box that my mum bought in Turkey. It has my name on it.
A man whose son was on the same train brought this one in. Is it yours?
Yes, that's it! It belongs to me. Thank you so much!
You're welcome. Please check everything's there, and sign here.

dialogue.focus: It's a brand-new blue backpack which has a pattern of white stars.
qs: What does Ali's backpack look like?
Who brought the backpack to the office?

speakout.scene: You've lost something important at the airport. I work at the lost and found office. Describe the thing and the place where you lost it in detail.

prompts.q: What did you lose, and what does it look like?
prompts.hint: Give the colour, size, pattern and what it's made of. Use 'which'.

prompts.q: Where do you think you left it behind?
prompts.hint: Describe the place with 'where' (for example, the café where I had breakfast).

prompts.q: How do I know it belongs to you?
prompts.hint: Describe something inside it or something special about it, using 'which' or 'that'.

culture.title: Lost Things Around the World
points: In Tokyo, people take millions of lost things to the police every year.
Some airports use special computer systems to find the owners of lost bags.
During Hajj, special teams help pilgrims who have lost their bags or their way.
qs: Have you ever left something behind? What happened?
What should you do if you find someone's wallet?

3-4.exit: Describe one thing you own in two sentences, so that someone can find it if you lose it. Use 'which' or 'that'.

3-5.objective: Today you will show a visitor around your city and describe people, places and things in detail.
3-5.warmup: What's the first place you'd show a visitor in your city?

expressions.def: found in a particular place
expressions.frame: My school is located in ___.

expressions.def: a famous building or place that is easy to recognise
expressions.frame: The most famous landmark in my city is ___.

expressions.def: having things all around
expressions.frame: My grandparents' farm is surrounded by ___.

expressions.def: from the area where you live
expressions.frame: A famous local dish in my city is ___.

expressions.def: the best or most exciting part of something
expressions.frame: The highlight of my last trip was ___.

expressions.def: something you buy to remember a place
expressions.frame: A good souvenir from my city is ___.

dialogue.scene: Hamad is a young volunteer guide in Riyadh. He is showing a visitor from Japan, Kenji, around the city.

p1.t: Welcome to Riyadh, Kenji! That tall tower is the Kingdom Centre, the most famous landmark in the city.
It's amazing! What's at the top?
A sky bridge which gives you a view of the whole city.
Great! What else should I see?

p2.t: Diriyah, which is located on the edge of the city. It's the place where the first Saudi state began.
What's the highlight there?
At-Turaif, an old district which is surrounded by mud-brick walls. Then we'll try some local food.
Perfect! And where can I buy a souvenir for my family?
Souq Al-Zal, where you can find old coins, carpets and Arabic coffee pots.

dialogue.focus: It's the place where the first Saudi state began.
qs: What can you see from the sky bridge?
What can Kenji buy at Souq Al-Zal?

speakout.scene: You're a tour guide in your own city or town. I'm a visitor from another country. Show me around and describe everything in detail.

prompts.q: What's the most famous landmark here?
prompts.hint: Name it and describe it with 'which' or 'where'.

prompts.q: Who are the people who make this place special?
prompts.hint: Describe local people or a famous person with 'who' or 'whose'.

prompts.q: What's a good souvenir, and where can I buy it?
prompts.hint: Describe the thing and the shop or market with 'which' and 'where'.

culture.title: Famous Landmarks
points: The Kingdom Centre in Riyadh is about 300 metres tall.
The King Fahd Fountain in Jeddah sends water more than 250 metres into the air.
The Eiffel Tower in Paris, which was built in 1889, is visited by millions of people every year.
qs: Which landmark would you show a visitor first? Why?
What's the best souvenir from Saudi Arabia, in your opinion?

3-5.exit: In two sentences, describe your city to a visitor. Use 'which', 'where' or 'who'.

words.ex: In my opinion, chess is more exciting than people think.
This puzzle game is so addictive that I forgot to eat lunch.
My dad thinks watching other people play games is a waste of time.
My mum checks my screen time every evening.
To be honest, I found the new game a bit boring.
What do you think about playing games online with strangers?

dialogue.t: Omar, that's three hours on that game! What do you think about your screen time today?
To be honest, it's a bit too much. But this new football game is really addictive.
In my opinion, three hours is a waste of time. It's a beautiful day outside.
Maybe, but it isn't a complete waste. I'm learning to work with my team online.
That's interesting. What do you think about playing real football instead?
Well, I think real football is better for my health, because I actually move.
Exactly. So let's go to the park after Asr. Dad can take us.
Fine! I'll save the game and come with you.

grammar.title: Giving opinions: I think / In my opinion
grammar.ar: نستخدم I think أو In my opinion قبل رأينا، ونضيف because لذكر السبب. وللسؤال عن رأي غيرنا: What do you think about + اسم أو فعل بـ ing؟
examples: I think this game is too difficult for young children.
In my opinion, reading is better than watching TV.
What do you think about playing games online?

words.ex: Personally, I prefer homemade sandwiches to canteen food.
I'm not keen on spicy food, but my brother loves it.
Fruit salad is a healthy option for break time.
What's your opinion of the new school timetable?
I believe that every student should drink more water.
The soup was tasteless, so nobody finished it.

dialogue.t: Noura, what's your opinion of the new canteen menu?
Personally, I'm not keen on it. The pasta was tasteless yesterday.
Really? I liked the chicken wrap. I believe it's a healthy option too.
Maybe, but they stopped selling samosas! That's a real shame.
In my opinion, it's good that they sell less fried food.
I suppose so. But I believe students should be able to choose.
What do you think about writing to the head teacher about it?
That's a great idea! Let's ask her to add fresh juice and dates.

grammar.title: Personally / I believe that / What's your opinion of …?
grammar.ar: Personally تعني رأيي أنا. بعد I believe نضع (that) + جملة كاملة. وWhat's your opinion of + اسم؟ سؤال مهذب عن الرأي.
examples: Personally, I love the canteen's falafel.
I believe that students need longer breaks.
What's your opinion of the new uniform?

words.ex: What did you think of the football match last night?
I found the book quite hard at first, but then I loved it.
Everyone loves that series, but I think it's overrated.
The plot was so confusing that I watched it twice.
How do you feel about films with sad endings?
The new animated film is worth watching with your family.

dialogue.t: So, Faisal, what did you think of the film?
I found it really funny, but the plot was a bit confusing in the middle.
Really? I thought the plot was clever. The ending surprised me.
True, the ending was great. But was the first film better?
To be honest, I think the first one is a bit overrated. This one was better.
I'm not sure. How do you feel about films with so many songs?
I usually skip the songs at home! But overall, it was worth watching.
In my opinion, it's the best film this year. Let's tell the whole family tonight!

grammar.title: Asking for opinions: What did you think of …? / How do you feel about …?
grammar.ar: بعد تجربة شيء نسأل: What did you think of …؟ وعن الشعور العام: How do you feel about …؟ والإجابة: I found it + صفة.
examples: What did you think of the new series?
How do you feel about very long films?
I found the ending really exciting.

words.ex: If you ask me, that was the best goal of the season.
The way I see it, the team needs a faster goalkeeper.
They didn't deserve to win; they only had one shot on goal.
It's unfair that the older boys always choose the teams.
The referee gave a yellow card to their captain.
Who do you think will score first tonight?

dialogue.t: That was never a penalty! The referee made a terrible mistake.
If you ask me, it was a penalty. The defender pushed him.
Well, it seems unfair. Al-Nassr played much better in the first half.
Maybe, but they missed so many chances.
So who do you think will win the league this year?
The way I see it, Al-Hilal has the strongest team, so they deserve to win.
I'm not sure. In my opinion, the league is very close this season.
We'll see! Quick, the second half is starting.

grammar.title: Strong opinions: If you ask me / The way I see it
grammar.ar: عبارات لإبداء رأي قوي، تأتي في أول الجملة ثم فاصلة ثم الرأي. وللسؤال عن التوقع: Who do you think will + فعل؟
examples: If you ask me, the coach should change the team.
The way I see it, they played better in the second half.
Who do you think will win the cup?

words.ex: It seems to me that our town needs more parks.
The mall was so crowded that we went home early.
My grandfather's farm is very peaceful in the evening.
There was a huge traffic jam after the match.
I'm not sure, but I think the new park opens next week.
There's a lot to do in Jeddah, like swimming and visiting old Al-Balad.

dialogue.t: Lama, what do you think about living in a small town?
I love it. It's peaceful, and my grandparents live next door.
It seems to me that small towns are a bit boring. In Riyadh there's a lot to do.
That's true, but Riyadh is so crowded. How long does it take you to get to your swimming club?
About forty minutes, because of the traffic jams every afternoon.
Forty minutes! I walk to my club in five.
OK, you win! But we have Riyadh Season, the Boulevard and huge malls.
I'm not sure, but I think a small town is still better for me. I'll visit you in winter, though!

grammar.title: Careful opinions: It seems to me that … / I'm not sure, but …
grammar.ar: It seems to me that تعطي رأياً بلطف وحذر. ونقول I'm not sure, but I think … عندما لا نكون متأكدين من رأينا.
examples: It seems to me that the traffic is getting worse.
I'm not sure, but I think small towns are safer.
It seems to me that there isn't a lot to do here for teenagers.

words.ex: From my point of view, school should start a bit later.
I'm convinced that reading every day makes you smarter.
What's your view on longer school holidays?
It makes sense to do your homework before you play.
There's a lot of pressure on players before a final.
The main reason I walk to school is the exercise.

dialogue.t: Welcome to School Radio! Should we get homework every day? Majed, what's your view on this?
From my point of view, a little homework every day makes sense. It helps us remember the lesson.
But many students say it's a waste of time. What do you think about that?
To be honest, some homework is boring. But the main reason we need it is practice.
Some parents say their children feel too much pressure. Is that true?
Sometimes, yes, especially before exams. If you ask me, twenty minutes a day is enough.
Interesting! So you're not against homework?
No. I'm convinced that short homework is better than no homework at all.

grammar.title: Opinions with reasons
grammar.ar: نقوّي رأينا بذكر السبب: The main reason is … . ونسأل عن رأي الآخرين: What's your view on …? ونعبّر عن قناعة قوية: I'm convinced that … .
examples: From my point of view, the school day is too long.
The main reason is that we're tired after lunch.
What's your view on online homework?

words.ex: A: I love mango juice. B: So do I!
A: I don't eat fish. B: Neither do I.
This chicken is too spicy for my little sister.
I'm in the mood for something sweet after dinner.
Choosing a favourite colour is just a matter of taste.
My brother hates waiting, and I feel the same way.

dialogue.t: I'm in the mood for kabsa. I love the chicken kabsa here.
So do I! It's the best kabsa in Dammam.
But I don't like it when the sauce is too spicy.
Neither do I. Last time my mouth was on fire!
What about dessert? I really like kunafa.
Really? I don't. It's too sweet for me. I prefer ice cream.
I can't believe it! Everyone likes kunafa.
Well, it's just a matter of taste. My sister feels the same way.

grammar.title: So do I / Neither do I
grammar.ar: نوافق على جملة مثبتة بـ So do I، وعلى جملة منفية بـ Neither do I. وإذا اختلفنا نقول: Really? I don't. أو Really? I do.
examples: A: I like dates. B: So do I.
A: I don't eat fish. B: Neither do I.
A: I love kunafa. B: Really? I don't.

words.ex: A: I'm tired of this heat. B: So am I!
A: I can't swim very well. B: Neither can I.
A: I've visited Abha twice. B: So have I.
I can't wait to see my cousins at Eid.
We go to Taif in summer for the cool weather.
We go camping in the desert every winter.

dialogue.t: I'm so tired of the heat in Riyadh. I can't wait for the summer holidays!
So am I! Dad says we can choose between Abha and Jeddah.
Hmm. I've been to Jeddah twice already.
So have I. Let's choose Abha this time. The cool weather there is amazing.
We could go camping in the mountains near Abha.
I'm not keen on that. I can't sleep well in a tent.
Neither can I, to be honest! Let's stay in a hotel and go camping for one night only.
Good idea. I can't wait to tell Mum and Dad.

grammar.title: Short answers: So am I / Neither can I / So have I
grammar.ar: في الرد القصير نستخدم نفس الفعل المساعد الموجود في الجملة: am ← So am I، can't ← Neither can I، have ← So have I.
examples: A: I'm tired. B: So am I.
A: I can't ride a camel. B: Neither can I.
A: I've seen that film. B: So have I.

words.ex: I see your point, but I still think school is more fun.
That's true, but the trip is very expensive.
You've got a point. We should leave early to avoid traffic.
It's better to say sorry face to face, not by message.
I can concentrate better in the library.
The TV is a big distraction when I do homework.

dialogue.t: I love learning to bake from online videos. I can watch them in my pyjamas!
Ha! I see your point, but I couldn't concentrate at all.
Why not? Your kitchen is so quiet.
Not when my little brothers are at home! They were a big distraction.
OK, you've got a point. But the videos are free, and we don't waste time in traffic.
That's true, but my cake was a disaster. I prefer learning face to face with a real chef.
So let's try the baking workshop at the mall, and watch videos at home too.

grammar.title: Disagreeing politely
grammar.ar: لا نقول You're wrong! بل نوافق على جزء من الفكرة أولاً ثم نعرض رأينا: I see your point, but … / That's true, but … .
examples: I see your point, but I learn better at school.
That's true, but online lessons can be boring.
You've got a point. Maybe we can do both.

words.ex: I totally agree that we should eat together as a family.
I'm afraid I don't agree. I think the rule is too strict.
A: Pets need lots of love. B: Exactly!
My cousin takes care of his grandfather's camels.
Feeding the birds is my responsibility.
Please don't make a mess in the kitchen.

dialogue.t: Dad, can we get a cat? All my friends have one!
Hmm. A cat is a big responsibility, Sara.
I totally agree. That's why I'll take care of it every day.
Every day? Even when we visit Grandma for the weekend?
Yes! And I'll clean its box. It won't make a mess, I promise.
I'm afraid I don't agree. Cats often make a mess with their hair and toys.
That's true, but we can brush it every week.
Well, you've got a point. Let's ask your mum first. Her opinion matters too.

grammar.title: Strong agreement and polite disagreement
grammar.ar: للموافقة القوية: I totally agree / Exactly!. وللاعتراض بأدب: I'm afraid I don't agree. كلمة I'm afraid هنا تجعل الاعتراض ألطف.
examples: I totally agree with you.
Exactly! That's what I think.
I'm afraid I don't agree. Cats are easy to keep.

words.ex: I couldn't agree more. We need more trees in our city.
You may be right, but it's too hot to walk to school.
A: New phones are always better. B: Not necessarily.
Our school recycles paper and cans.
Turning off the lights can make a big difference.
Many shops have stopped giving single-use plastic bags.

dialogue.t: Look at all these plastic bottles in the water! We should stop using single-use plastic.
I couldn't agree more. It's terrible for the fish and turtles.
But two boys with a net can't make a difference.
You may be right, but if every family on every boat does this, it will help.
True. My family recycles paper and bottles now.
So does mine! But recycling isn't enough. We need to use less plastic.
Not necessarily. If you ask me, bags you can use again and again are the best.

grammar.title: Agreeing and disagreeing in discussions
grammar.ar: I couldn't agree more = موافقة تامة. You may be right, but … = موافقة جزئية ثم اعتراض. Not necessarily = ليس دائماً صحيحاً.
examples: I couldn't agree more. Plastic is a big problem.
You may be right, but recycling is expensive.
A: Big cars are safer. B: Not necessarily.

words.ex: I'm with you on that. The zoo is perfect for younger students.

words.w: I'm not so sure about that.
words.ex: I'm not so sure about that. It might rain tomorrow.
Fair enough. Let's leave the beach for winter.
The majority of students voted for the museum.
I wanted the red bike, but then I changed my mind.
After a long talk, my brothers and I came to an agreement.

dialogue.t: OK, we have three choices: Ithra, the beach in Al-Khobar or a farm trip. What do you think?
Ithra, definitely. It has a library, a museum and a cinema.
I'm with you on that. But some players say it's boring.
I'm not so sure about that. They have fun science shows for kids.
The beach is fun too. Lots of the players love swimming.
That's true, but it's very hot this month. We can go to the beach in winter.
Fair enough. Let's ask the team and see what the majority wants.
Good idea. And if they choose the farm, maybe I'll change my mind!

grammar.title: Reaching an agreement
grammar.ar: في النقاش نوافق (I'm with you on that)، ونشكّك بأدب (I'm not so sure about that)، ونقبل الرأي الآخر (Fair enough) حتى نصل إلى اتفاق.
examples: I'm with you on that. Ithra is a great choice.
I'm not so sure about that. The farm is very far.
Fair enough. Let's ask the majority.

words.ex: Khalid fell out with his cousin over a video game.
Why don't you call him and say sorry?
The twins argued in the morning but made up by lunch.
He apologised for being late to the match.
Have you tried talking to your teacher about it?
She was upset because nobody remembered her birthday.

dialogue.t: What's wrong, Omar? You look upset.
I fell out with Yousef. I laughed when he missed a penalty, and now he won't talk to me.
Oh no. Have you tried talking to him?
Yes, but he walked away. What should I do?
Why don't you apologise? Tell him you're really sorry you laughed.
But it was just a joke!
Maybe for you, but not for him. You could send him a message tonight.
OK, I'll try. I really want to make up with him before Thursday's match.

grammar.title: Making suggestions
grammar.ar: Why don't you + فعل؟ اقتراح لطيف. You could + فعل = يمكنك أن. Have you tried + فعل بـ ing؟ = هل جرّبت؟
examples: Why don't you invite him to play?
You could write her a short note.
Have you tried asking your teacher for help?

dialogue.t: Hind, I'm so stressed out. I have four exams next week!
Don't worry, that's normal. Have you started to revise?
A bit, but I'm falling behind in maths. I don't know where to start.
If I were you, I'd make a timetable. Write which subject you'll study each day.
Good idea. But I study for hours and still forget everything.
Then take a break every forty minutes. Your brain needs rest.
Really? I thought breaks were a waste of time.
Not at all! And if I were you, I'd ask your teacher for extra maths exercises.

grammar.title: If I were you, I'd + verb
grammar.ar: عبارة ثابتة للنصيحة: If I were you (لاحظ were مع I) ثم I'd أو I wouldn't + فعل في صيغته الأساسية.
examples: If I were you, I'd go to bed early.
If I were you, I wouldn't study all night.

dialogue.t: Faisal, you look exhausted. Are you OK?

Why don't you put your phone away an hour before bed? You'll fall asleep faster.
OK. And what about breakfast? I usually just eat crisps.
That's junk food! If you eat eggs or labneh and bread, you'll have more energy.
Fine, I'll try to get into the habit of eating a proper breakfast.

grammar.title: First conditional for advice

grammar.title: You'd better / It's a good idea to / unless
grammar.ar: You'd better + فعل = نصيحة قوية (وإلا ستحدث مشكلة). It's a good idea to + فعل = نصيحة لطيفة. unless = إلا إذا (أي if not).

dialogue.t: Noura, can I ask your advice? I start at my new school on Sunday.

stories.title: The Man in the Dark Room

pages.text: In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, a boy called Yusuf worked for a baker near the great mosque of Al-Azhar. Every morning, he carried warm bread to a house at the end of a narrow street. People in the market said that the man inside was very strange. "He sits in the dark all day," the baker warned him. "Leave the bread at the door, and don't ask him any questions."

One morning, the door was open, and Yusuf heard a calm voice from inside. "Come in, young man, but close the door quickly!" The room was completely dark except for one tiny hole in the wooden shutter of the window. Yusuf's heart was beating fast, but he was curious, so he stepped inside.

Then he noticed something amazing on the white wall. He could see the street outside, with all its colours and people moving! But everything was upside down. A camel was walking slowly across the wall with its feet in the air. "Is this magic?" Yusuf whispered.

The man laughed kindly. "No, it isn't magic. It's light. My name is Al-Hasan Ibn al-Haytham, and I have been studying light for many years." He explained that light travels in straight lines, so the light from the camel's head passes through the hole and lands at the bottom of the wall. "Never believe something just because a famous book says it," he added. "Test it with your own eyes."

After that day, Yusuf visited the scholar whenever he had free time. Ibn al-Haytham did experiments with candles, mirrors and bowls of water, and he wrote down every result carefully. In those days, many people believed that our eyes send out rays so that we can see. "If that were true, we could see in the dark," Ibn al-Haytham said. "Light comes into our eyes from the world, not the other way round."

One windy evening, while Ibn al-Haytham was praying at the mosque, a candle fell onto a pile of his papers. Yusuf was sweeping the floor when he smelled smoke. Without stopping to think, he grabbed a bowl of water and threw it over the flames. His hand was slightly burned, but most of the pages were safe.

When the scholar came back, he stared at the wet, black edges of his papers for a long time. "These pages are ten years of my life," he said quietly. "You have saved them, Yusuf." From then on, he taught the boy to write neatly, and Yusuf helped him to copy his great work, the Book of Optics.

Many years later, the book was translated into other languages and studied by scholars for hundreds of years. Even today, cameras work in the same way as that dark room in Cairo. Yusuf, now an old man with grandchildren, often told them, "I knew him. He taught me to ask questions." And whenever Yusuf saw sunlight shining through a small hole, he smiled.

pages.text: Every afternoon after school, Faisal climbed the stairs to the roof of his family's house in Riyadh. There, next to his mother's plants, stood his homemade weather station: a thermometer, a small wind vane and an old barometer that his uncle had given him. He wrote every number carefully in a blue notebook. "One day, I'm going to be a real meteorologist," he often told his little sister, Noura.

On Thursday evening, Father announced some exciting news. "Tomorrow we're going to the desert with Grandfather and your cousins," he said. "We'll set up the tent, cook dinner and watch the stars." Faisal checked the weather forecast on his tablet, and it said: sunny, light winds, no rain.

The next afternoon, the camp was full of noise and laughter. The boys were playing football on the red sand while Grandfather made coffee over the fire. But Faisal had brought his barometer, and when he looked at it, he frowned. The pressure was falling fast, faster than he had ever seen before.

"I think the weather is going to change," Faisal told his cousin Saad. Saad laughed and pointed at the sky, which didn't have a single cloud in it. "Your little machine is broken, Faisal!" But Faisal noticed that the birds had disappeared, and the hot air felt strangely heavy and still.

Faisal ran to Grandfather, who was sitting quietly by the fire. The old man listened, then stood up and looked towards the west for a long time. Far away, a thin brown line was growing along the horizon. "The boy is right," Grandfather said calmly. "A sandstorm is coming, so we must leave now."

Everyone packed as quickly as they could, and within ten minutes the cars were moving towards the main road. Through the back window, Faisal watched a huge wall of dust rise into the sky, as tall as a mountain. Then it hit them, and suddenly the afternoon turned orange, then almost black. Father switched on the lights and drove slowly, while strong gusts of wind shook the car and sand hissed against the glass.

After half an hour, the wind became weaker and the sky slowly cleared. The family waited at a petrol station until the roads were safe, and then drove home. The next morning, Father and Grandfather went back to the camping place. The tent had been blown away, and the fireplace was completely buried under the sand. "I'm sorry I laughed at your machine," Saad told Faisal quietly.

That evening, Grandfather climbed the stairs to the roof for the first time in years. "When I was young, I read the sky with my eyes," he said, "but you read it with numbers too." Faisal smiled and showed him how the barometer worked, and Grandfather taught him the names of the winds that his own father had taught him. From that day, the blue notebook had two kinds of notes: Faisal's numbers and Grandfather's stories about the sky.

His barometer showed the pressure falling fast

pages.text: Faris Al-Harbi had a secret that nobody at school knew. He loved art more than any other subject, and his notebooks were full of sketches of old buildings and fishing boats. But when he looked at a red apple and a green leaf, they seemed almost the same colour to him. He was colour-blind, and he was afraid that people would laugh if they found out.

One Sunday morning, Mr Saeed, the art teacher, made an announcement. "Our school is going to paint a huge mural on the wall by the gate," he said. "The theme is 'Our City', and the best design will be chosen by a team of judges next Thursday." The students cheered, and Faris felt his heart beat faster. Then he remembered the colours, and his excitement quickly turned into worry.

That evening, he visited his grandfather in Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. Grandfather had spent forty years carving wooden windows called rawasheen for the tall coral houses. "Why the long face?" he asked, putting down his tools. Faris took a deep breath and told him everything about the competition and his problem with colours.

Grandfather smiled and led him to an old window at the top of the stairs. "Look carefully," he said. Sunlight was shining through the carved wood, and it drew beautiful patterns of light and shadow across the floor. "I have never needed a single colour to make something beautiful," Grandfather explained. "Light, shadow and shape can tell a story too."

For the next four days, Faris worked on his design every afternoon. He used blues and yellows, which he could see clearly, and many dark and light shades. His picture showed the old houses of Al-Balad, with the shadows of the rawasheen falling across a quiet street. His best friend Omar looked at it and said, "It looks like the sun is really shining on the paper!"

On Thursday, all the designs were hung in the school hall. Most students had used every colour in the box: bright red cars, green palm trees and orange sunsets. Faris's picture looked very different, and some boys whispered that he had forgotten his colours. He wanted to hide, but instead he stepped forward bravely when the judges reached his work.

"Why did you choose only two colours?" asked one of the judges, a well-known artist from the city. Faris's voice shook a little as he answered. "I'm colour-blind, so I can't see reds and greens well. My grandfather taught me that light and shadow can be just as powerful as colour." The hall went completely silent, and then the artist began to nod slowly.

Faris's design won first prize, and the judges said it was the most original picture they had seen that year. A month later, the mural was finished, and every morning its painted shadows welcomed the students at the gate. Grandfather came to see it, leaning on his stick and smiling proudly. "You see," he said, "you didn't lose any colours. You found a new way of seeing."

options: Everyone was surprised and moved by his honest answer.

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef stayed at his grandfather's old house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. One hot afternoon, while he was looking for a fan in the storeroom, he found a dusty wooden box. Inside, there was an old camera with a leather strap. A tiny number on the top showed that only two photos were left.

Yousef pointed the camera at the window and pressed the button. There was a bright white flash, and the room seemed to spin around him. When he opened his eyes, he was standing in a narrow street full of tall houses with carved wooden balconies. There were no cars, no phones and no air conditioners, only the smell of the sea and the shouts of men selling fish.

Suddenly, a boy about his age came running round the corner and crashed into him. An envelope fell from the boy's hand, and Yousef picked it up. "Thank you!" the boy said, out of breath. "I'm Saleh. My father's letter must reach Captain Hamid before his ship leaves at noon, but I'm new in Jeddah and I've taken a wrong turn."

Yousef's heart was beating fast, but he wanted to help. His grandfather had told him many stories about these streets, and he recognised the tall white tower of a famous old house. "The port is this way," he said confidently. "If we hurry, we can still make it!"

The two boys ran past busy shops and through a crowded market until they could see the blue water. A large ship was already pulling up its heavy anchor. "Captain Hamid!" Saleh shouted, waving the envelope above his head. A tall man with a grey beard turned, smiled and took the letter just before the ship began to move.

"You saved my family's shop," Saleh said. "That letter was a big order, and without it, my father would have lost everything. What's your name?" Yousef smiled and said, "Just call me a friend." Saleh looked down and laughed, "Your shoes are very strange, friend!" Yousef held the camera at arm's length, took a photo of them together, and the white flash filled the air again.

Yousef was back in the dusty storeroom, holding the camera. At that moment, his grandfather walked in and went completely silent when he saw it. "When I was your age," he said slowly, "a boy with strange shoes and a camera exactly like this one helped me deliver an important letter. I never saw him again, so years later I bought this camera to remember him." Then he looked carefully at Yousef's shoes, and his eyes grew wide.

The next day, they took the film to a small photo shop, and the owner printed the last picture. It showed two smiling boys standing by the sea, with a ship sailing away behind them. Grandfather Saleh held the photo with shaking hands. "I have waited fifty years to say thank you," he said softly, and Yousef hugged him tightly. "You're welcome, my friend," he answered.

pages.text: Every Friday morning, Faisal went fishing with his grandfather on the Red Sea coast near Yanbu. They always took their small boat past the mangroves, strange trees that grow in salty water with their roots standing up like fingers. "These trees are older than me," Grandfather said. "They protect the coast from storms, and baby fish hide between their roots." Faisal nodded, but secretly he thought they were just ugly bushes.

One Friday, Grandfather turned off the engine and frowned. The water near the trees was full of rubbish: plastic bottles, bags, and an old fishing net caught in the roots. Suddenly, something moved under the net. Faisal leaned over the side of the boat. "Grandfather, look! It's a turtle!" he shouted.

The turtle was trapped, and one of its front legs was wrapped tightly in the net. It was trying to swim, but it was getting tired. Grandfather handed Faisal a small knife. "Cut carefully, close to the net, not near the leg," he said calmly. Faisal's hands were shaking, but he held the net still and began to cut.

After a few long minutes, the last piece of net fell away. The turtle rested for a moment, then pushed its strong legs against the water and disappeared into the blue. Faisal laughed with relief, but Grandfather looked sadly at the rubbish around them. "When I was your age, this water was so clear that you could see every fish," he said. "Now people throw everything away and forget that the sea remembers."

That night, Faisal couldn't sleep. He searched online and discovered that mangroves store more carbon than many forests on land, and that they were disappearing in many countries. He also found photos of turtles that had not been as lucky as his. In the morning, he took his laptop to school and showed his science teacher, Mr. Khalid.

"If we do nothing, more animals will get hurt," Faisal explained to his class. Mr. Khalid suggested a clean-up day, and soon thirty students had signed up. Some parents offered boats, and a local fishermen's group promised to collect the old nets. Even Faisal's little sister, Noura, made posters that said, "The sea is not a bin!"

On Saturday, the beach was busy with families wearing gloves and carrying bags. They worked all morning in the hot sun, pulling plastic out of the roots and the sand. By lunchtime, they had filled more than two hundred bags. A reporter from the local newspaper took photos and asked Faisal why he had organised the event. "Because these trees look after the sea," he said, "so we have to look after them."

A few weeks later, Faisal and Grandfather took the boat out again. The water between the mangroves was clean, and tiny silver fish were swimming between the roots. Then a familiar shape rose to the surface, with a small scar on its front leg. Faisal smiled and waved as the turtle swam past. "You know," he told his grandfather, "I think these trees are actually quite beautiful."

stories.title: The Night Fixer of Al-Ward Street

pages.text: When Rakan's family moved to Abha, nothing seemed to go right for him. On his first week, his bicycle got a flat tyre, and he had no money to repair it. He left it next to the wall of their building and went to bed in a bad mood. The next morning, he couldn't believe his eyes: the tyre was full of air and the chain was shining.

"Did Dad fix it?" Rakan asked his older sister, Jana. "No, he left for work before sunrise," she replied. Over the next few days, more strange things happened on Al-Ward Street. The broken bench near the mosque was painted green, and the noisy gate of the school stopped making its terrible sound.

"Someone is fixing our street at night," Jana said, her eyes wide. "Let's find out who it is!" They made a plan to stay awake on Thursday night and watch from their window. Rakan took a notebook to write down everything they saw, like a real detective.

Just after midnight, a thin shadow appeared under the streetlight. It was an old man carrying a heavy toolbox, and he was walking slowly towards the water pipe that had been leaking for weeks. Rakan whispered, "That's Uncle Idris from the ground floor! He never talks to anyone." They watched quietly as he worked carefully until the water stopped dripping.

In the morning, they told their father about it. He smiled sadly and explained that Uncle Idris had been a mechanic for forty years. "Since his wife passed away, he has been living alone, and I think he finds it hard to sleep," he said. Jana looked at her brother and said, "He has been kind to everyone, but has anyone been kind to him?"

That afternoon, the two of them wrote a letter that said, "Thank you, Night Fixer. We know your secret!" They put it in an envelope with a small box of their mother's date biscuits. Rakan knocked on the old man's door, then both of them ran away, laughing nervously. From behind a car, they saw Uncle Idris open the door, read the letter, and touch his eyes.

The next Friday, their father invited Uncle Idris to lunch after the prayer. At first he was shy, but soon he was telling funny stories about the old cars he had repaired. "I thought nobody noticed what I did," he admitted quietly. "Of course we noticed," Rakan said. "Our street is better because of you."

Now, every Saturday morning, Rakan and Jana help Uncle Idris with his repairs, and he teaches them how to use his tools. He doesn't have to work in the dark anymore, because he isn't alone. Sometimes neighbours bring him tea or ask for his advice, and he always smiles. Rakan has learned that kindness is like a good tool: the more you use it, the more useful it becomes.

options: Kindness should be returned and shared with others.

pages.text: Faisal had always thought the desert was empty. That changed on the first night of the winter holiday, when Uncle Khalid drove him and his sister Noura deep into the Nafud to join the family camp. "Grandfather is already there," Uncle Khalid said, smiling. "He's making his famous coffee."

An hour later, the sun was going down, and the red dunes looked like waves of fire. Suddenly the car shook and stopped, and the back wheels were stuck deep in the soft sand. Uncle Khalid jumped out to look, but he stepped on a rock and twisted his ankle. "Don't worry," he said, although his face showed pain.

Faisal checked his phone, but there was no signal at all. The car's map screen showed only a blue dot in the middle of nowhere. "The camp is about three kilometres north of here," Uncle Khalid said. "I can't walk that far with this foot." Noura looked at Faisal, and he knew exactly what she was thinking.

"We can go and bring help," Noura said. Uncle Khalid was worried at first, but finally he agreed, because it was getting cold quickly. He gave them a torch, a bottle of water and his thick jacket. "Stay together, and if you get lost, come straight back to the car lights," he told them.

The children climbed the first dune, but when they reached the top, every direction looked the same. The sky had turned dark, and thousands of stars appeared above them. Faisal suddenly remembered something Grandfather had taught him last summer. "Look for the star that never moves," Grandfather had said. "Our grandparents used it to find their way for hundreds of years."

Faisal searched the sky until he found a shape like a big spoon. He followed its two front stars upwards to a small, bright star standing alone. "That's Al-Jadi, the North Star!" he shouted. "If we walk towards it, we'll reach the camp." They started walking, checking the star every few minutes so they would not lose their way.

The walk was harder than they had expected, because their feet sank into the sand with every step. When Noura began to feel tired, Faisal held her hand and told her stories to keep her going. After almost an hour, they heard a sound in the distance. It was the soft music of an oud, and then they saw the orange light of a fire.

Grandfather stood up in surprise when the two children walked out of the darkness. Soon the uncles drove out with ropes and found Uncle Khalid, who was cold but safe. Later, sitting by the fire with a cup of warm milk, Faisal looked up at Al-Jadi again. "You remembered," Grandfather said proudly. Faisal smiled, because now he understood that the desert was never empty: it was full of stars, stories and paths for anyone who knew how to read them.

options: Its back wheels were stuck in soft sand.

options: He was too tired after driving.

options: He used the map on his phone.

options: He now sees the desert in a new and richer way.

pages.text: Every August, Lina and her younger brother Faisal spent a week at their grandfather's house on the Red Sea coast, not far from Umluj. Grandfather Saeed had been a fisherman for forty years, and he knew the sea better than anyone. Lina loved his stories, but this summer he had promised them something better than a story. "This year," he said with a smile, "you will see a secret with your own eyes."

On the first morning, he led them along the beach to a small circle of white stones. "Two months ago, a green turtle came out of the sea here at night," he explained. "She dug a deep hole, laid about a hundred eggs, and then went back to the water." Faisal stared at the sand. "Are they still down there?" he whispered. "Yes," said Grandfather, "and I think they will hatch very soon, maybe even tonight."

After dinner, the family walked quietly back to the nest. "No torches and no phones," Grandfather warned. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the brightest light, and that should be the moon shining on the water." But Lina noticed something worrying further down the beach. A new café had opened there, and its strong white lights were shining across the sand like a football stadium.

Just before midnight, the sand inside the circle began to move. First one tiny head appeared, then another, and suddenly dozens of baby turtles were climbing out, each one no bigger than Lina's hand. "They're amazing!" Faisal breathed. Then Lina's smile disappeared. Instead of heading towards the waves, the turtles were turning the wrong way, towards the café and the busy road behind it.

"Stay with Grandfather!" Lina told Faisal, and she ran across the sand as fast as she could. At the café, the owner was carrying a tray of tea to his customers. Out of breath, Lina explained about the turtles and the lights. The man frowned. "If I switch them off, my customers won't be able to see anything," he said. "Please," Lina begged. "If you don't, they'll die on the road before they ever reach the sea."

For a moment, the owner said nothing. Then an old man at one of the tables stood up. "My son, the girl is right," he said calmly. "We can drink our tea in the dark for a few minutes." The owner nodded, walked to the wall and pressed a switch, and the whole beach went dark.

Slowly, Lina's eyes got used to the darkness, and she saw the silver path of the moon on the sea. One by one, the little turtles stopped, turned around and began hurrying towards the water. Faisal and Grandfather walked beside them, making sure that crabs and birds stayed away. When the last turtle disappeared into the waves, Faisal said proudly, "I counted eighty-seven!" Behind them, the café customers began to clap.

The next evening, the family went back to the café and found a surprise. The owner had replaced the bright white lights with soft orange ones that pointed away from the beach, and a new sign said: "Turtle nesting area – please keep the beach dark." "Only one baby turtle in a thousand grows up," Grandfather told the children, "but the females return to the beach where they were born." Lina looked out at the moonlit sea and smiled, imagining a big green turtle climbing onto this same sand, many years from now.

options: To show where the turtle eggs were

options: He wanted to protect the turtles in the future

pages.text: Faisal was twelve, and he was the youngest member of his school's radio club in Riyadh. One Sunday morning, Mr. Khalid, their teacher, walked into the room with a huge smile. "Our school has been chosen," he said. "Next Thursday, we are going to talk to an astronaut on the International Space Station!" Each student could ask one question, and Faisal already knew what his would be.

Mr. Khalid explained that the space station travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. "It will appear over the horizon at 8:14 in the evening," he said. "After ten minutes, it will disappear again, so we can't waste a single second." Faisal wrote his question on a small card and practised it every night: "What does Earth look like at night from space?"

On Thursday afternoon, the sky suddenly turned orange. A strong dust storm swept across the city, and the wind shook the windows of the school. By the time it had finished, the families were already arriving in the hall for the big event. Then Mr. Khalid came back from the roof, and his face was pale. "The antenna is bent," he said quietly. "Without it, we won't hear anything."

Faisal remembered the summer he had spent helping his grandfather repair an old radio in the village. "Sir, can I help?" he asked. Mr. Khalid hesitated, then nodded, and together they climbed the stairs to the roof. Dust was still blowing in the air, so they covered their faces and worked quickly. Using strong tape and a metal pole from the storeroom, they managed to make the antenna stand straight again.

At 8:14, everyone in the hall held their breath, but the speaker made only a soft hissing noise. A minute passed, and still there was nothing. Faisal looked at the map on the wall and suddenly realised the problem. "The station is coming from the north-west, but the storm turned the antenna to the east!" He and Mr. Khalid ran back upstairs and turned it as fast as they could.

When they returned, a clear, friendly voice was filling the hall. "Hello, Riyadh! This is the International Space Station. Can you hear me?" The students cheered, and then, one by one, they stepped up to the microphone. They asked how astronauts sleep, what food they eat, and whether they ever feel homesick.

At 8:22, the signal was getting weaker, and Faisal was the last in line. His hands were shaking as he read his card. There was a long crackle, and he thought he had been too late. Then the astronaut answered, "Right now, I can see the lights of your city shining like gold, and a long cloud of dust beside them. Thank you for not giving up tonight."

A moment later, the voice disappeared, and the whole hall stood up and clapped. Later that night, Faisal and his father went up to the roof of their house. At exactly the right time, a bright point of light moved silently across the dark sky. Faisal waved at it, even though he knew no one could see him, and his father laughed and waved too.

options: Because Faisal asked a very long question
Because she knew the students had faced problems but kept trying
Because the families had waited a long time in the hall

pages.text: Faisal had been captain of the Al-Nakheel Junior team for two seasons, and he was proud of his loud voice. "Pass! Man on! Shoot!" he shouted at every training session, and everyone listened. One Sunday afternoon, Coach Saleh walked onto the pitch with a tall, thin boy carrying a blue bag. "This is Omar," the coach said. "He's just moved here from Abha, and he's going to play with us."

Omar was fast, and he could control the ball as if it was glued to his feet. But during the practice match, something strange happened. Faisal shouted "Behind you!" three times, and Omar didn't turn around. A defender took the ball easily, and Faisal threw his arms in the air. "Why don't you listen?" he said angrily.

After training, Coach Saleh took Faisal aside. "Omar can't hear, Faisal," he explained quietly. "He was born deaf, but he reads lips and uses sign language." Faisal's face went hot with shame. He had been angry with a boy for something that wasn't his fault.

The next day, Faisal waited for Omar by the school gate and said sorry slowly, so Omar could read his lips. Omar smiled and typed a message on his phone: "No problem, but shouting doesn't help me. Maybe we need a new language." That evening, the two boys sat on the roof of Faisal's house and invented signals for the team. A closed fist meant "defend", a pointing finger meant "pass to me", and a hand on the head meant "far post".

At first, some of the players laughed and said the signs were silly. "Real footballers shout," said Hamad, the goalkeeper. But after two weeks of practice, the team was playing better than ever. They didn't waste their breath, and the other teams never knew what they were planning.

The final of the city cup was played in a big stadium, and thousands of families had come to watch. The noise was unbelievable, with drums, horns and cheering from every side. Faisal tried to shout to his defenders, but even he couldn't hear his own voice. The score was 1-1, and there were only two minutes left.

Then the referee blew his whistle: a free kick for Al-Nakheel, just outside the box. Faisal stood over the ball and looked across at Omar, who was waiting near the defenders. Without a word, Faisal put his hand on his head. Omar nodded and moved quietly towards the far post, while the defenders watched the wrong players.

Faisal curled the ball high over the wall, and Omar met it with a perfect header. The net shook, and the stadium exploded with noise. Omar couldn't hear the crowd, but he could see his whole team running towards him, making a new sign with their hands: the one for "thank you". Later, holding the cup, Faisal smiled. He had always believed that a captain needed a loud voice, but now he knew that the best leaders also know how to listen.

options: The coach was not at the match.
