questions.q: What lesson did Faisal learn by the end of the story?
options: A captain must always shout the loudest.
Good leaders also listen and understand others.
Signals are only useful for deaf players.

pages.text: Every summer, Yusuf stayed with his grandfather in the old part of Jeddah called Al-Balad. The house was more than a hundred years old, with tall white walls and beautiful wooden windows called roshans. Yusuf loved its narrow stairs and cool, shady rooms. But this summer, something strange began to happen.

On his first night, Yusuf was reading in bed when he heard it: tap, tap, tap… tap. The sound came from inside the wall, right next to the wooden window. He held his breath and listened, but after a few minutes it stopped. "It's just an old house," Grandfather said at breakfast, smiling. "Old houses like to talk."

But the tapping came back the next night, and the night after that. When Yusuf's cousin Hamad arrived at the weekend, Yusuf told him everything. "Maybe it's a mouse," Hamad suggested. "A mouse can't tap the same way every time," Yusuf replied. "Let's keep a notebook and write down exactly when it happens."

For three evenings, the boys sat in the room with a torch and a notebook. They noticed that the tapping never started at exactly the same minute. However, it always began soon after sunset, and it stopped when the night became completely still. On the third evening, Hamad pointed at the curtain. "Look, it's moving!" he whispered.

Suddenly, Yusuf understood. "It's the wind from the sea," he said. "Every evening the breeze comes in through the roshan, and something inside the wall moves." The boys examined the wooden panel under the window carefully and discovered that one piece was loose. When Yusuf pressed it gently, it slid to the side.

Behind the panel was a small, dark space. A thin piece of metal hung from a nail, and every time the wind blew, it knocked against an old tin box. Hamad held the torch while Yusuf carefully lifted the box out. It was covered in dust, and on the lid someone had scratched two letters: S and K.

Inside, they found a few glass marbles, a faded photograph of two smiling boys, and a folded letter. The letter said: "To my brother Khalid. When you find this, remember our promise. Your brother, Saad." The boys looked at each other in surprise. Grandfather's name was Khalid!

Grandfather looked at the photograph for a long time, and his eyes filled with tears. "Saad and I hid our treasures in this house when we were boys," he said softly. "We promised we would always stay close, but life got busy, and we haven't spoken for years." That evening, he picked up the phone and called his brother in Madinah. For the first time that summer, there was no tapping in the wall, only the happy sound of two brothers laughing together.

questions.q: Where did Yusuf hear the tapping sound?
options: Inside the wall next to the wooden window
On the stairs outside his room

questions.q: Why did the boys keep a notebook?
options: To draw pictures of the old house
To write down exactly when the tapping happened
To make a list of things to buy

questions.q: What was really making the tapping sound?
options: A mouse living in the wall
A piece of metal moved by the wind, knocking against a box
Grandfather knocking on the wall at night

questions.q: In the story, the night became 'completely still'. What does 'still' mean here?
options: Quiet, with no wind or movement

questions.q: Why do you think Grandfather's eyes filled with tears?
options: The dust in the box hurt his eyes
He remembered his brother and their old promise
He was angry that the boys opened the wall

stories.title: The Star That Led Us Home

pages.text: Saad and Talal had been best friends since they were six years old. But for two whole weeks, they hadn't spoken a single word to each other. At the school football final, Saad had missed an important penalty, and when he looked up, he saw Talal with his hand over his face, shaking. Saad was sure his best friend was laughing at him.

Now their two families were going camping together in the desert, as they did every winter. The fathers set up the big tent near the red sand dunes, while the mothers made Arabic coffee and served dates. Talal sat alone on a rock, cleaning his old telescope. "You two used to be like brothers," Saad's father said quietly. "Why don't you go and talk to him?"

Saad pretended he hadn't heard and walked towards a rocky hill to take photos of the sunset. After a few minutes, he heard footsteps behind him. He turned around and saw Talal. "Why are you following me?" Saad asked angrily. "My father says nobody should walk alone in the desert," Talal replied, looking at the ground.

The sun disappeared much faster than they expected, and soon the sky was dark. On the way down, Talal slipped on a loose stone and twisted his ankle badly. He cried out in pain and couldn't stand up. Saad took out his phone, but there was no signal, and the lights of the camp were hidden behind the tall dunes.

Saad's heart was beating fast, and he felt very scared. "Do you remember what I showed you last summer?" Talal asked, pointing up at the sky. "That bright star is the North Star, and our camp is north of this hill." Saad remembered the long nights when Talal had taught him the names of the stars. He helped his friend stand up and put Talal's arm over his shoulder.

They walked slowly, step by step, while the stars shone above them. "At the final, I wasn't laughing at you," Talal whispered. "I was crying, but I covered my face because I didn't want anyone to see. I hate losing, and I felt terrible for you." Saad stopped walking. "I'm so sorry," he said. "I should have asked you instead of being so stubborn."

Suddenly, they saw the lights of torches moving across the sand, and they heard voices calling their names. It was their fathers, who had been searching for them for almost an hour. Saad's father hugged both boys tightly. Back at the tent, Talal's mother checked his ankle carefully and smiled with relief, because it was only a sprain.

Later, the two friends sat by the warm fire, drinking hot milk with cardamom. Talal handed Saad his precious telescope. "Next time we come camping, you can be the guide," he said. Saad laughed and looked up at the North Star. "Deal," he replied. "And next time, we ask each other before we stop talking."

questions.q: Why did Saad stop talking to Talal?
options: He thought Talal was laughing at him after he missed a penalty.
Talal broke his phone during the football final.
Talal refused to go camping with his family.

questions.q: What happened to Talal on the way down the hill?
options: He lost his telescope in the sand.
He slipped and twisted his ankle.

questions.q: How did the boys know which way to walk back to the camp?
options: They followed the sound of the fire.
They used a map on Saad's phone.
They used the North Star, because the camp was north of the hill.

questions.q: In the story, the word "stubborn" means someone who…
options: refuses to change their mind or behaviour.
is very kind and helpful to others.

questions.q: What can we understand from the ending of the story?
options: The boys will never go camping again.
The boys learned that friends should talk honestly instead of guessing.
Saad wants to keep Talal's telescope forever.

stories.title: The Girl Who Caught the Clouds

pages.text: Every morning in the mountains of Asir, a thick white mist covered Grandpa Saleh's village. Layan loved walking through it on her way to school, because it felt like walking inside a cloud. But this year the rain was late, and the water tank behind Grandpa's house was almost empty. His small garden of mint and pomegranate trees was slowly turning brown.

One evening, Layan was reading a science magazine when she saw a photo of a small black beetle. "Omar, look at this!" she called to her younger brother. "This beetle lives in the Namib Desert in Africa, where it hardly ever rains. Every morning it stands on top of a sand dune, and tiny drops of fog collect on its back and run down into its mouth." Omar laughed. "So it drinks the air?"

"Not exactly," said Layan, her eyes shining. "The air carries millions of tiny water drops, and if we can catch them, we can water Grandpa's garden." The next day, they found an old fishing net and two long wooden poles in the storeroom. With Grandpa's help, they tied the net between the poles on the hill and placed a bucket underneath.

At sunrise, the children ran up the hill, full of hope. The mist was thick, and the net looked wet and silver. But when they looked inside the bucket, there were only a few drops at the bottom. "It didn't work," Omar said sadly, kicking a stone.

Layan didn't give up. She studied the net closely and noticed that the holes were too big, so most of the mist was passing straight through. She also saw that the drops were falling onto the ground instead of into the bucket. "We need smaller holes and a way to guide the water," she explained.

Grandpa listened carefully and then smiled. He brought out a roll of green shade cloth that he used to protect his plants from the sun. Omar cut a plastic pipe in half to make a gutter along the bottom of the cloth, so that every drop would slide into the bucket. That night, they all went to bed wondering what the morning would bring.

When the call to Fajr prayer woke them, the mist was already drifting over the hill. After praying, they hurried outside with a torch. Water was dripping steadily from the cloth into the gutter, and the bucket was nearly half full! Omar jumped with excitement, and Grandpa laughed so loudly that the neighbour's goats looked up.

Within a week, the fog catcher was collecting about ten litres of water every morning, which was enough to save the mint and the pomegranate trees. Layan entered the project in the regional science fair and won first prize. When the judges asked who had taught her, she smiled. "A tiny beetle," she said, "and a grandfather who never stopped believing in us."

questions.q: Why was Grandpa's garden turning brown?
options: The rain was late and the water tank was almost empty.
The goats were eating the plants.
The sun was too strong for the mint.

questions.q: What gave Layan the idea to catch water from the mist?
options: A story her grandfather told her.
A photo of a beetle in a science magazine.
A lesson about rain at school.

questions.q: Why did the first fog catcher fail?
options: The poles broke in the wind.
There was no mist that morning.
The holes were too big and the drops fell on the ground.

questions.q: In the story, what does "steadily" mean in "Water was dripping steadily"?
What can we understand about Layan from the story?
options: She learns from mistakes and keeps trying.
She prefers to work alone without help.
She is not interested in science.

pages.text: Reem had always thought the Empty Quarter was just sand, sand and more sand. So when her uncle Khalid, a scientist who studied rocks, invited her on a three-day trip there, she almost said no. "Bring a hat, a notebook and lots of patience," he told her with a smile. In the end, her curiosity was stronger than her doubts.

On the second morning, they drove between dunes as tall as buildings. Abu Nasser, their guide, had crossed this desert since he was a boy, and he never needed a map. He stopped the car near a flat, white area covered in small stones. "Long ago, this was a lake," Uncle Khalid explained. "Thousands of years ago, there was water, grass and animals here."

Reem laughed. "Here? Not even a bird could live here!" She walked away to explore, keeping her eyes on the ground. Suddenly, something small and brown was shining between the stones. She brushed away the sand and found a tooth almost as big as her hand.

Uncle Khalid's eyes went wide. "This could belong to a hippo," he whispered. But Abu Nasser was looking at the sky, not at the tooth. Far away, a yellow wall was moving quickly towards them. "Sandstorm," he said calmly. "Into the car, now."

For two hours, the wind screamed around them, and they couldn't see anything through the windows. Reem held the tooth tightly and tried not to be afraid. To pass the time, Abu Nasser told stories about his grandfather, who used the stars to find wells at night. "The desert takes things, and the desert gives things," he said. "We just have to wait."

When the wind finally stopped, the world looked different. A whole dune had moved, and the shape of the land had changed. Then Reem noticed long, curved bones sticking out of the ground where the wind had blown the sand away. "Uncle," she said quietly, "I think the storm has found the rest of your hippo."

They spent the afternoon carefully taking photos, measuring the bones and recording the exact location with GPS. Uncle Khalid called the university, and his voice was shaking with excitement. "Nobody has ever found a complete skeleton in this area before," he said. Abu Nasser just smiled. "You see? The desert gives things."

Six months later, Reem stood in a museum in Riyadh in front of a large glass case. Inside was the hippo skeleton, and next to it was a small sign with her name on it. Visitors stopped to read about the ancient lake in the Empty Quarter. Reem opened her notebook and wrote: "Never say a place is empty. You just haven't looked carefully enough."

questions.q: What did Reem find first between the stones?
Why did Abu Nasser tell everyone to get into the car?
options: He wanted to drive to a well

questions.q: What does the word "ancient" mean in the story?
How did the sandstorm help them?
options: It showed them the way home
It blew away the sand and uncovered the bones
It brought water to the old lake

questions.q: What has Reem learned by the end of the story?
options: That the desert is always dangerous
That she should never go on trips with her uncle
That a place can hold surprises if you look carefully

pages.text: The first time the doorbell rang, Yousef jumped up from the sofa and ran to the front door. He opened it with a big smile, expecting the pizza delivery. But there was nobody outside, only the hot afternoon wind and a cat sitting on the wall. Behind him, from the living room, someone laughed.

The laugh came from Sultan, Grandma's grey parrot. Sultan had lived with the family for three years, and he was very clever and very noisy. He could already say "Assalamu alaikum" and "Where are my glasses?" in Grandma's voice. Now, it seemed, he had learned a new sound: ding-dong.

Over the next week, the doorbell rang about twenty times a day. Dad ran to the door in the middle of his lunch. Noura, Yousef's older sister, put on her best scarf and went to the door because she thought her friend had arrived. Even Mum, who was usually very calm, started to look nervous whenever she heard a ding. Sultan looked very pleased with himself.

"We have to do something," Dad said one evening. "Yesterday the real delivery man rang three times, and nobody opened the door because we thought it was the bird." Yousef had an idea: if Sultan heard different sounds, maybe he would forget the doorbell. So he played whale songs, piano music and even a recording of camels to the parrot for hours. Sultan just looked at him and said, "Where are my glasses?"

Then Sultan learned more tricks. He copied Mum's phone, so everyone searched under the cushions for a phone that wasn't ringing. He copied the microwave, so Noura kept opening it and finding nothing inside. Worst of all, he copied Dad's voice shouting, "Yousef! Homework!" and Yousef sat down at his desk every time before he realised the truth.

One afternoon, Yousef came home early and heard a strange sound from Grandma's room. He looked quietly through the open door. Grandma was sitting next to the cage with a small bell in her hand. "Ding-dong," she whispered, and rang it. "Ding-dong," Sultan answered happily.

"Grandma!" Yousef said. "Was it you all the time?" Grandma's face turned a little pink, but then she started laughing so much that her glasses fell off. "Everyone in this house stays on the sofa with their phones all day," she explained. "When the doorbell rings, at least you all stand up and walk. I've been giving the whole family free exercise!"

That night, Yousef told everyone, and the living room filled with laughter. Dad decided to buy a new doorbell that played a short song instead of a ding-dong. The next morning, it played its happy tune for the first time, and the whole family smiled. But by lunchtime, a familiar voice from the living room was singing the same song perfectly.

questions.q: What did Yousef expect to find when he first opened the door?
Why did nobody open the door for the real delivery man?
options: They thought the sound came from Sultan

questions.q: In the story, Mum started to look "nervous". What does "nervous" mean?
Why did Grandma teach Sultan the doorbell sound?
options: She wanted the family to move and stop sitting with their phones
She wanted to win a parrot competition
She couldn't hear the real doorbell

questions.q: What can we guess from the last sentence of the story?
options: Dad returned the new doorbell to the shop
Sultan had already learned the new doorbell song
Grandma started singing in the living room

pages.text: Yousef had been waiting all summer for this trip. His uncle Khalid was a marine scientist who studied sea turtles near the Farasan Islands in the Red Sea. "Today you're not a passenger," his uncle said as the boat left the harbour. "You're my assistant, so keep your eyes open."

On the laptop, a small green dot was flashing on a map of the sea. "That's Noura," Uncle Khalid explained. "She's a green turtle, and we put a tracker on her shell last year." Every hour the tracker sent a signal, so the scientists always knew exactly where she was swimming.

After a while, Yousef noticed that the green dot wasn't moving. "Has the battery died?" he asked nervously. His uncle frowned and looked closely at the screen. "The signal is still working, but she hasn't moved for almost an hour. If she's in trouble, we need to find her quickly."

They followed the signal towards a small reef. The wind was getting stronger, and dark clouds were appearing in the west. Captain Saeed, who had sailed these waters for thirty years, shook his head. "We have one hour, maybe less, before the waves get dangerous."

Yousef put on his mask and leaned over the side of the boat. Through the clear blue water, he saw something terrible. Noura was trapped in an old fishing net that was caught on the coral. She was pulling hard, but every movement made the net tighter.

Uncle Khalid dived in with a knife, and Yousef held the rope that connected him to the boat. Turtles can hold their breath for a long time, but not forever. Yousef's heart was beating fast as he counted the seconds. At last his uncle came up, holding a piece of torn net in his hand.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then Noura moved her flippers slowly and swam away into the deep blue. Yousef shouted with joy, and even Captain Saeed was smiling. "Now let's go home," the captain said, "before the sea changes its mind."

That evening, back at the research centre, Yousef sat with his uncle in front of the laptop. The green dot was flashing again, moving steadily north. "You did well today," Uncle Khalid said. "Real scientists don't just watch the ocean - they protect it." Yousef smiled, because he already knew what he wanted to be.

questions.q: What was Uncle Khalid's job?
options: He was a marine scientist who studied sea turtles.
He was a fisherman who sold fish in the harbour.
He was a captain who sailed boats for thirty years.

questions.q: Why did Yousef and his uncle start to worry about Noura?
options: The battery in the laptop died.
Her signal showed she hadn't moved for almost an hour.
She swam too close to the boat.

questions.q: In the story, what does the word "trapped" mean?
Why did Captain Saeed want to hurry?
options: A storm was coming and the waves could become dangerous.
He wanted to catch more fish before dark.
The boat did not have enough fuel.

questions.q: What can we guess about Yousef at the end of the story?
options: He never wants to go on a boat again.
He wants to become a scientist who protects the ocean.
He wants to keep Noura as a pet.

pages.text: In Al-Ahsa, Faisal's grandfather had a date farm with more than two hundred palm trees. Every weekend, Faisal helped him check the trees and collect the sweet, golden dates. But this summer, something was wrong. One of the oldest palms was turning yellow, and nobody knew why.

"It's the red weevil," Grandfather said quietly, touching the trunk. "It's a small insect that lives inside the tree and eats it from the inside. By the time you see the damage, it's usually too late." Faisal looked up at the tired leaves. He had never seen his grandfather look so worried.

That night, Faisal couldn't sleep. He kept thinking about an enemy that nobody could see. Then he remembered something from science class: doctors use a stethoscope to listen to the heart. "If I can't see the weevils," he thought, "maybe I can hear them."

The next morning, he borrowed an old stethoscope from his aunt, who was a nurse. He pressed it against the sick tree and held his breath. At first there was only silence. Then he heard it: a tiny crunch, crunch, crunch, like someone eating crisps very slowly.

Faisal decided to build a better listening machine. He used a small microphone, an old phone and a free app that showed sounds as lines on the screen. His older sister Noura, who was good at coding, helped him write a program that beeped whenever it heard the crunching sound. It took them three weeks and many failed attempts, but finally the machine worked.

They tested it on every tree on the farm. Most trees were quiet, but the machine beeped loudly at four palms that still looked completely healthy. Grandfather raised his eyebrows. "Those trees are fine," he said. "Are you sure your machine isn't broken?"

Faisal asked him to trust the invention. A farm expert came to check, and when he made a small hole in the first tree, he found weevils inside. Because they had found the insects early, the expert was able to treat all four trees and save them. Sadly, the old yellow palm could not be saved.

In winter, Faisal and Noura showed their invention at the national science fair in Riyadh and won second prize. But for Faisal, the real prize came later, back on the farm. Grandfather planted a young palm where the old one had stood. "This one," he said, smiling, "will grow up with a doctor who can hear its heart."

questions.q: Why was Grandfather worried at the beginning of the story?
options: One of his oldest palm trees was turning yellow.
He had no time to collect the dates.
Faisal did not want to help on the farm.

questions.q: What gave Faisal the idea for his invention?
options: A video he watched on his phone
Remembering how doctors listen to the heart
A book his sister gave him

questions.q: In the story, what does "attempts" mean?
Why did Grandfather think the machine might be broken?
options: It made no sound at all.
It beeped at trees that looked healthy.

questions.q: What does Grandfather's final sentence show?
options: He wants Faisal to become a real doctor.
He is still angry about losing the old palm.
He is proud of Faisal and trusts his invention.

pages.text: Faisal had never been on a train before, so he was awake long before his alarm rang. Today he and his grandfather were travelling north from Riyadh to Al-Jouf, where his uncle grew olives. "The journey takes about eight hours," Grandpa said as they found their seats. "When I first made it, it took me three days."

As the train left the station, Grandpa took a small brown notebook out of his bag. Its cover was torn and its pages were yellow, but every page was full of tiny drawings and neat writing. "I was nineteen when I wrote this," he explained. "I travelled with a truck driver who carried dates to the north."

Faisal turned the pages carefully. There was a drawing of a well where camels drank, a sketch of a broken tyre, and a map of a road that disappeared into the sand. "Let's play a game," Grandpa suggested. "Look out of the window and try to find the places in my notebook." Faisal pressed his face against the glass, but everything looked new and different.

Around midday, the sky slowly turned orange. The wind grew stronger, and soon the window looked as if someone had painted it with sand. The train slowed down and finally stopped. A voice announced that there was a sandstorm ahead and that the journey would be delayed for at least two hours.

Some passengers sighed, and a businessman complained loudly on his phone. Across the aisle, a little boy started crying because the battery in his tablet had died. Faisal looked at the notebook in his hands and had an idea. "Grandpa," he whispered, "you were stuck in a sandstorm once, weren't you? It's on page twelve."

Grandpa smiled and began to tell the story. He described how the truck had got stuck in a sand dune, how they had waited all night under the stars, and how a Bedouin family had shared hot tea and bread with them in the morning. The little boy stopped crying and moved closer. Soon, half the carriage was listening, and even the businessman had put his phone away.

When Grandpa finished, the passengers wanted more, so he told them about the broken tyre and the camel that refused to move. Time passed so quickly that everyone was surprised when the train began moving again. "Back then, a storm cost us a whole day," Grandpa laughed. "Today it cost us two hours and gave us a party!"

That evening, they arrived in Al-Jouf, where Uncle Saad was waiting with a basket of fresh olives. Before going to sleep at the farm, Faisal opened a brand-new notebook he had bought at the station. On the first page, he drew a train standing still in an orange storm, surrounded by smiling faces. Underneath he wrote: "Some journeys are measured in kilometres. The best ones are measured in stories."

questions.q: How long did Grandpa's first journey to the north take?
Why did the train stop in the middle of the journey?
options: The train had a broken tyre
A camel was standing on the tracks

questions.q: In the story, the journey "would be delayed". What does "delayed" mean?
Why did Faisal remind Grandpa about the story on page twelve?
options: He wanted to check if Grandpa remembered his notebook
He thought the story could make the bored and upset passengers feel better
He was frightened and wanted to know how to escape

questions.q: What does Faisal mean by his final sentence in his notebook?
options: Long journeys are always better than short ones
People should count kilometres carefully when they travel
The stories and people we meet make a journey special

pages.text: Omar had always been the slowest boy in his class at football. When the teams were chosen, his name was always called last. So when Coach Hamad started an archery club at school, Omar joined, mostly to escape the football pitch. He didn't expect to love it.

The bow was heavier than it looked, and his first arrows flew everywhere except the target. "Don't fight the bow," Coach Hamad said. "Breathe in, hold, and let the arrow go while you breathe out." Omar practised every afternoon, even when the sun was hot and the other boys had gone home.

Slowly, his arrows began to land closer to the centre. Coach Hamad noticed something else too: Omar always watched the flags on the fence before every shot. "You're reading the wind," the coach said, smiling. "Not many archers your age think about that."

In March, the school was invited to a regional competition in Taif. Omar was chosen for the team, together with his friend Yousef, who was the best archer in the club. The night before, Omar couldn't sleep. He kept imagining his arrows missing the target while hundreds of people watched.

On the day, a strong wind was blowing across the field. Many archers were having problems, and Yousef's first three arrows landed far to the left. He looked pale and worried. "The wind is coming from the mountains," Omar whispered to him. "Aim a little to the right, and wait until the flags go quiet."

Yousef tried it, and his next arrow hit the yellow centre. Then Omar stepped up for his own final round. His hands were shaking, but he remembered the coach's words: breathe in, hold, breathe out. He watched the flags, waited for the wind to drop, and released the arrow.

When the results were announced, Yousef had finished second, and Omar was fourth, just one point away from a medal. For a moment, Omar felt disappointed. Then Yousef walked over and put his silver medal around Omar's neck. "Half of this is yours," he said. "I would have finished last without you."

Omar laughed and gave the medal back, but he couldn't stop smiling on the bus home. Coach Hamad sat down beside him. "Next year, I want you to help me train the new archers," he said. "A good archer hits the target, but a great one helps others see the wind." Omar looked out of the window at the palm trees moving in the breeze, and he was already reading it.

questions.q: Why did Omar first join the archery club?
options: He wanted to get away from football
His father told him to join
He had won an archery medal before

questions.q: What did Omar do before every shot that surprised his coach?
options: He watched the flags to read the wind

questions.q: In the story, "Yousef looked pale" means that he looked...
What position did Omar finish in at the competition?
Why do you think Coach Hamad asked Omar to help train new archers?
options: Because Omar won a gold medal
Because Omar understood the wind and helped his friend
Because Omar was the oldest boy in the club

stories.title: The Robot That Listened to the Palms

pages.text: Every Friday, Huda visited her grandfather's farm in Al-Ahsa, where hundreds of date palms stood in long green lines. This year, however, she brought a guest: a small robot on six wheels, with a long metal arm and two round lights for eyes. She had spent three months building it for the school science fair. "Grandpa, meet Sahm," she said proudly.

Grandpa Saleh looked at the robot for a long time, then laughed. "I have looked after these palms for fifty years without a machine," he said. "The trees speak to me, and I listen." Huda smiled, but she didn't give up. "Sahm listens too, Grandpa. It pushes its arm into the soil and tells me if the roots are getting enough water."

That afternoon, while Grandpa was resting after lunch, Huda sent Sahm along the rows of palms. The robot moved slowly, stopping at each tree to test the ground. Near the eastern wall, its eyes suddenly turned red, and it started beeping loudly. The screen on Huda's tablet showed a strange message: "Soil too wet. Water loss."

Huda ran to tell her grandfather, but he only shook his head. "That's impossible," he said. "I watered that corner yesterday, the same as every other corner. Your robot must be broken." Huda felt disappointed, and on the drive home she wondered if he was right.

The next Friday, Grandpa called her before she had even left the house. "Bring your robot," he said quietly. "The palms in the eastern corner don't look well, and I don't understand why." When Huda arrived, she saw that several trees had yellow leaves, and the ground beneath them was dark and soft.

Sahm rolled forward and tested the soil again, moving in a careful circle. Each time, the red light grew brighter, until finally the robot stopped next to one old palm and refused to move. Grandpa fetched a shovel and began to dig. Half a metre down, they found an old pipe with a long crack, and water was escaping into the earth.

"The roots were drowning," Grandpa said, wiping his forehead. "A few more weeks, and these trees would be dead." That evening, he repaired the pipe with help from a neighbour, and he looked at Sahm in a new way. "Maybe your machine has good ears after all," he admitted with a smile.

A month later, Huda's project won second prize at the science fair. Sitting proudly in the front row was Grandpa Saleh, wearing his best thobe. When the judges asked where the robot had been tested, he stood up before Huda could answer. "On my farm," he said. "The palms speak to me, and now Sahm helps me hear them better."

questions.q: Why did Huda build Sahm?
options: To pick dates from the palms

questions.q: What did Grandpa Saleh think when he first heard Sahm's warning?
options: He thought the robot was broken
He thought the trees needed more water
He thought a neighbour had damaged the pipe

questions.q: In the story, "the roots were drowning" means the roots had…
What was the real problem in the eastern corner?
options: An old pipe with a crack under the ground
The well had no water in it

questions.q: How had Grandpa's feelings about Sahm changed by the end of the story?
options: He trusted the robot and was proud of it
He still believed machines were useless
He wanted to sell the robot to his neighbour

stories.title: The Lantern at Station Number Nine

pages.text: Faisal had never been excited about museums, but the Hejaz Railway Museum in Madinah was different. The building was an old train station made of dark stone, and a real steam engine stood outside it like a sleeping giant. "Before this railway was built in 1908," the guide explained, "the journey from Damascus to Madinah took about forty days by camel. By train, it took only four." Faisal whistled quietly. That was faster than some school holidays!

Inside, the walls were covered with black-and-white photographs. Faisal stopped in front of one that showed six railway workers standing beside the tracks in the desert. One tall man was holding a metal lantern with a round handle and a tiny star cut into its side. Faisal leaned closer, and his heart started beating faster. He had seen that exact lantern before, hanging on the wall of his grandfather's majlis.

That evening, Faisal ran straight to his grandfather's house. "Jaddi, where did your old lantern come from?" he asked, almost out of breath. His grandfather smiled slowly, as if he had been waiting years for this question. He took a small key from his pocket and opened a wooden box that Faisal had never been allowed to touch. Inside lay a faded notebook with a cover as soft as cloth.

"This belonged to my grandfather, Hamad," Jaddi said gently. "He was a signalman at a small desert station on the railway, Station Number Nine." A signalman's job was to warn the drivers about danger on the tracks, especially at night. Faisal opened the notebook carefully. The handwriting was neat but old-fashioned, and the pages smelled of dust and history.

One entry was longer than the others, and Jaddi read it aloud. "Tonight a terrible sandstorm arrived without warning. When the wind finally stopped, I discovered that sand had completely covered the tracks north of the station. The night train from the north was due in less than an hour, and it was carrying more than two hundred passengers." Faisal held his breath and waited for the next line.

"I took my lantern and ran along the tracks into the dark," the notebook continued. "When I saw the engine's light, I waved the lantern from side to side again and again. The driver saw my signal just in time, and the train stopped only a few metres from the sand." Jaddi closed the notebook. "No one was hurt that night," he said proudly, "because of one man and one small light."

The next week, Faisal and his grandfather took the lantern and the notebook to the museum. The manager, Dr. Noura, read the story twice and then looked at the photograph on the wall. "We never knew the names of these workers," she said with shining eyes. "Would your family allow us to display these objects? Visitors should know what Hamad did." Jaddi looked at Faisal, and Faisal nodded immediately.

A month later, Faisal's class returned to the museum. In a glass case beneath the old photograph, the lantern glowed softly, and a small sign read: Hamad bin Saad, Signalman, Station Number Nine. This time, Faisal was the guide, and he told the whole story without looking at any notes. When he finished, his classmates clapped, and Jaddi, standing at the back, wiped a tear from his eye. Faisal realised that history isn't only in books; sometimes it's hanging on your grandfather's wall.

questions.q: How long did the journey from Damascus to Madinah take by train?
Why did Faisal's heart start beating faster at the museum?
options: He saw a lantern in a photo that looked like his grandfather's
He got lost from his class

questions.q: What does the word "faded" mean in "a faded notebook"?
options: Old, with colours that are no longer strong

questions.q: What problem did Hamad discover after the sandstorm?
Why do you think Jaddi wiped a tear from his eye at the end?
options: He was proud that his grandfather was finally remembered
He was sad to lose the notebook forever

pages.text: Every summer, Lina and her younger brother Omar spent two weeks at their grandfather's house by the Red Sea. This year, something was different. A new café had opened at the end of the beach, and at night its bright white lights shone across the sand like a small sun. "The beach used to be so peaceful," Grandfather said, shaking his head.

One evening, while they were walking along the shore after dinner, Omar stopped suddenly. "Look! The sand is moving!" he whispered. Lina bent down and saw tiny dark shapes climbing out of a hole near the rocks. They were baby turtles, and each one was no bigger than her hand.

At first, Lina felt excited, but then she noticed something strange. The turtles weren't going towards the water. Instead, they were crawling up the beach, towards the café and the busy road behind it. "Why are they going the wrong way?" Omar asked.

Lina remembered a lesson from her science teacher, Miss Huda. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the brightest light," she explained quickly. "Usually that's the moon shining on the water, but tonight the café lights are much brighter." If they didn't do something soon, the turtles would reach the road.

"Omar, stay here and don't let anyone step on them," Lina said, and she ran towards the café as fast as she could. The owner, a tall man called Mr Saeed, was carrying a tray of drinks. Lina was out of breath, but she told him everything. For a moment he looked confused, and then he put down the tray and hurried to the light switch.

One by one, the lights went out, and the beach became dark and quiet. Some customers complained, but Mr Saeed explained what was happening, and soon everyone was standing silently, watching. Slowly, the little turtles turned around. Above the sea, the moon was shining, and its silver path on the water was showing them the way home.

Grandfather had come with his torch, but he kept it switched off. "We mustn't touch them," he said softly. "They need to make this journey by themselves." Lina counted forty-three turtles as they disappeared into the waves, and she didn't breathe properly until the last one had gone.

The next week, Mr Saeed replaced his white lights with soft red ones that turtles can't see easily, and he put up a sign about the nest. "You taught me something important," he told Lina. "In twenty years, some of those turtles will come back to this same beach to lay their own eggs," Grandfather added proudly. Back at school, Lina wrote her science project about that night. She called it "Follow the Moon," and Miss Huda gave it the highest mark in the class.

questions.q: What did Omar see moving on the sand?
Why were the turtles going towards the road?
options: They were following the bright café lights
They were afraid of the waves

questions.q: In the story, "Lina was out of breath" means that she...
options: was very angry with Mr Saeed

questions.q: Why did Grandfather keep his torch switched off?
options: He wanted to save it for later
Its light might confuse the turtles

questions.q: What can we guess about Mr Saeed at the end of the story?
options: He was still angry with Lina
He cared about protecting the turtles
He decided to close his café

pages.text: Noura was looking for a pencil in the kitchen drawer when she found an old card covered in her grandmother's handwriting. At the top it said, "Teta's Date Ma'amoul." Noura smiled, because nobody made ma'amoul like her grandmother. But when she read the list of ingredients, her smile disappeared: a brown coffee stain covered one important word. All she could read was "one spoonful of..."

The next morning, her teacher announced a Family Recipe Competition for Thursday. "Bring a dish that has a story," Ms. Reem said. Noura knew immediately what she wanted to make. There was just one problem: Teta was in Makkah for Umrah, and her phone was always switched off. Noura sent her a message anyway, but no answer came.

On Monday evening, Noura decided to guess the missing ingredient. "It must be cinnamon," she told her little brother, Saad, as she mixed the dough. When the biscuits came out of the oven, Saad took one bite and made a terrible face. "These taste like a candle shop," he said honestly. Noura laughed, but inside she felt worried.

On Tuesday, she tried ginger instead, but the ma'amoul tasted hot and strange. "They're nice," said her mother kindly, "but they aren't Teta's." Noura sat down on the kitchen floor with flour all over her hands. The competition was in two days, and she still hadn't solved the mystery. "Maybe I should just buy biscuits from the bakery," she said quietly.

"Before you give up," her mother said, "why don't you look in Teta's spice cupboard?" Noura opened the little wooden door, and a warm, sweet smell surrounded her. She lifted the lids one by one until she found a small glass jar with green seeds inside. As soon as she smelled it, she remembered Eid mornings in her grandmother's house. "Cardamom!" she shouted, and Saad came running to see what had happened.

Noura turned the card over and noticed a short line she had never seen before: "Leave the dough to rest all night. Good food can't be hurried." So on Wednesday evening, she made the dough carefully and covered it with a clean cloth. She set her alarm for five o'clock and went to bed feeling excited and nervous at the same time. Early the next morning, the whole house smelled exactly like Teta's kitchen.

At school, the hall was full of delicious dishes, from spicy kabsa to golden luqaimat. The judge, a famous chef called Huda, walked slowly from table to table. She tasted one of Noura's ma'amoul and closed her eyes for a moment. "There's a secret in this recipe," she said. "Can you tell me what it is?" Noura thought carefully and answered, "Cardamom, and a lot of patience."

Noura didn't win first prize, but Chef Huda gave her a special award for the Best Family Story. That evening, her phone finally rang, and Teta's happy face appeared on the screen. "I saw your message," her grandmother said. "Did you find the missing word?" Noura held up a plate of ma'amoul and smiled. "I found two," she said, "and next time, Teta, we'll bake them together."

questions.q: Why couldn't Noura read the whole recipe?
options: A coffee stain covered one word
The card was torn in half
The writing was in a different language

questions.q: Why didn't Teta answer Noura's message at first?
options: She was in Makkah and her phone was switched off

questions.q: What does "give up" mean in the story?
How did Noura discover the missing ingredient?
options: She read it on the internet
She smelled the jars in Teta's spice cupboard

questions.q: Why did Noura say she found "two" missing words at the end?
options: She learned that both cardamom and patience were important
She made two kinds of biscuits

pages.text: Huda had always loved sounds more than silence. Every morning she listened to the seagulls over the Jeddah Corniche, the hiss of her grandmother's coffee pot and the slow tick of the old clock in the hall. One day, her music teacher, Ms. Reem, announced a competition called "The Music Around Us," and Huda's heart jumped. "Create a piece of music using only real sounds from your life," Ms. Reem explained. "The winner will perform at the school's end-of-year celebration."

That evening, Huda borrowed her father's phone and started recording everything. She recorded rain tapping on the car window, her little brother's laughter and the bubbling of rice in a huge pot. Her grandmother watched her with curious eyes. "What are you collecting, my dear?" she asked. "Music, Grandma," Huda replied, as she held the phone close to a dripping tap.

For two weeks, Huda worked on her laptop every night after she had finished her homework. She cut the sounds into tiny pieces and arranged them like notes in a song. The drip of the tap became a drum, and the coffee pot sang like a flute. Slowly, her ordinary house was turning into an orchestra. By Wednesday night the piece was finally complete, and she went to bed feeling proud.

The next morning, disaster struck. When Huda opened her laptop, the screen stayed black, and nothing happened when she pressed the buttons. Her brother had accidentally knocked a glass of water onto the keyboard the night before. "All my sounds are gone," she whispered, as tears filled her eyes. The competition was that afternoon.

Grandma sat down beside her and took her hand. "The sounds aren't inside that machine," she said gently. "They're still here, in this house and in this city. You only need to find them again." Huda looked up slowly, because an idea was forming in her mind, and it was a little crazy.

At school, Huda explained her plan to her three best friends, Lama, Sara and Noura. Instead of playing a recording, they would make every sound live, in front of everyone. Huda had brought a metal tray, a bowl of water, an empty glass bottle and a bag of dried beans. They practised in an empty classroom at lunchtime and laughed whenever someone made a mistake. "If we don't keep the rhythm, it will sound terrible," Lama warned.

When their turn came, the hall went quiet. Noura shook the beans like falling rain, Sara dropped water into the bowl, and Lama tapped the tray softly. Then Huda blew across the top of the bottle, and it hummed like a flute. The audience leaned forward, completely amazed, because for three minutes the stage sounded exactly like Huda's home on a rainy morning.

When they finished, there was a moment of silence, and then the whole hall exploded with applause. Ms. Reem was smiling widely when she announced the winners. That night, Huda told Grandma everything, and Grandma laughed until her eyes were wet. "You see?" she said. "A machine can break, but your ears will always find the music." Outside the window, the rain had started to play again, and Huda smiled.

questions.q: What did the competition ask students to do?
options: Play a famous song on an instrument
Make music using only real sounds from their lives
Write a story about their favourite singer

questions.q: Why did Huda's laptop stop working?
options: Her brother knocked water onto the keyboard
She dropped it on the floor

questions.q: In the story, "disaster struck" means that...
Which object did Huda use to make a sound like a flute on stage?
What does Grandma's advice teach Huda?
options: The music she needs is all around her, not only in a machine
She should buy a new laptop quickly

pages.text: Every morning that week, Grandma Huda found her mint plants in a mess. The pots on the balcony had been knocked over, and some leaves had disappeared completely. "Someone is stealing my mint," she said, holding her cup of tea. Her granddaughter Layan, who loved detective stories, put down her book. "Don't worry, Grandma. I'll solve this case."

Layan opened a new notebook and wrote "Suspects" at the top of the page. The first name was Bader, her little brother, because he loved mint in his tea and often woke up early. The second suspect was Mishmish, the neighbour's orange cat, who sometimes walked along the wall. "I didn't touch anything!" Bader said angrily when she asked him. "That's exactly what a thief would say," Layan replied, but she wasn't completely sure.

Next, she searched the balcony carefully for clues. There was soil on the floor, a few small twigs and one grey feather near the door. Strangely, the leaves hadn't been eaten, and the stems looked as if someone had pulled them off. Layan took photos with her phone and wrote down everything she noticed.

That evening, she had a clever idea. She borrowed some flour from the kitchen and spread a thin layer around the plant pots. "If anyone comes tonight, they'll leave footprints," she explained to Grandma. Bader rolled his eyes, but he promised to stay in bed until the sun came up.

In the morning, Layan ran to the balcony before breakfast. Two more mint plants had been attacked, and the flour was covered in tiny marks. They weren't the round prints of a cat, and they certainly weren't the prints of a boy's bare feet. Each one looked like a little arrow, with three thin lines pointing forward.

Layan compared the prints with pictures on the internet, and suddenly her eyes lit up. "It's a bird!" she shouted, remembering the grey feather and the twigs. Grandma laughed. "So our thief has wings!" But one question was still bothering Layan: why would a bird want mint?

Just after sunrise the next day, she hid behind the curtain with Bader. A grey pigeon landed, pulled at a mint stem with its beak and flew up to the top of the air conditioner. There, hidden in the shadows, was a nest with two small white eggs. "She's building a home for her babies," Bader whispered. "Maybe she likes the smell of mint," Layan said with a smile, "just like you."

Layan crossed out both names on her list and said sorry to her brother. The family decided not to chase the pigeon away. Instead, they moved Grandma's best plants inside and left one pot of mint on the balcony just for the bird. Two weeks later, when two fluffy babies appeared in the nest, Layan wrote in her notebook: "Case closed. A good detective follows the evidence, not her first guess."

questions.q: What was happening to Grandma Huda's mint plants?
options: They were knocked over and leaves were missing every morning
They were drying because nobody watered them
Someone moved them inside the house at night

questions.q: Why was Bader the first name on Layan's list of suspects?
options: He had broken a plant pot before
He loved mint in his tea and often woke up early
Grandma saw him on the balcony at night

questions.q: What does the word "clues" mean in the story?
options: Small plants that grow on a balcony
Things that help you find the answer to a mystery

questions.q: How did Layan know the cat was not the thief?
options: The cat was sleeping at home all night
The neighbour told her the cat was inside
The prints in the flour were not round like a cat's prints

questions.q: What lesson did Layan learn at the end of the story?
options: You should never leave plants on a balcony
You should follow the evidence instead of your first idea
Birds are more dangerous than cats

pages.text: Yousef had always loved superhero comics, but he never expected to become a hero himself. One Thursday evening, while he was carrying a tray of tea glasses to his grandfather, he tripped over the edge of the carpet. The tray flew into the air, and without thinking, he clapped his hands. Suddenly everything stopped: the glasses, the drops of tea, and even the cat in the middle of a jump.

Five seconds later, the world started moving again, but by then Yousef had already caught every single glass. His grandfather was looking at him strangely over his newspaper. "You're very quick tonight," he said calmly, and he went back to his reading. Yousef's heart was beating so fast that he could hear it in his ears.

For the whole week, Yousef practised secretly on the roof of their house. He soon discovered the rules of his strange power. Each clap froze the world for exactly five seconds, and afterwards he felt as tired as he did after a long football match. He chose a hero name, "Pause," and he imagined his photo on the front page of every newspaper in the country.

On Friday afternoon, the family went to the Corniche for a picnic. Yousef couldn't relax because he was waiting for a chance to show his power. "Why are you staring at everyone like that?" asked his cousin Huda, who was eating sunflower seeds. "No reason," he answered. "I'm just keeping an eye on things."

Then he heard a scream that made his blood go cold. A little boy's ball had rolled towards the road, and the boy was chasing it, right in front of a fast car. The driver hadn't seen him yet. Yousef jumped up and clapped as hard as he could.

The world went silent, and the car and the boy were frozen like statues. Yousef ran faster than he had ever run before, counting in his head: one, two, three. On four, he lifted the boy back onto the pavement, and on five, everything moved again. The car passed safely, and the boy's mother ran over and held her son tightly, crying, "Thank God, thank God!"

Nobody had noticed Yousef at all. People were saying that the boy had been very lucky, and soon everyone returned to their picnics. Yousef sat down on a bench, completely exhausted. He had wanted to be famous, but strangely, he didn't feel disappointed, because the mother's smile was worth more than any newspaper photo.

A moment later, his grandfather sat down beside him and handed him a bottle of cold water. "Five seconds isn't much time," he said quietly, "but it's enough if you use it well." Yousef stared at him, and before he could ask a question, his grandfather slowly clapped his hands, and the seagulls froze above the waves. "Our family has kept this secret for a very long time," the old man said with a smile. "Welcome, Pause."

questions.q: What happened the first time Yousef used his power?
options: He stopped a car on the road
He saved a cat from the roof

questions.q: What happened to Yousef each time he used his power?
In the story, what does "exhausted" mean?
Why didn't Yousef feel disappointed when nobody noticed him?
options: He was afraid people would laugh at him
He didn't want his cousin to know
Seeing the mother happy meant more to him than fame

questions.q: What can we guess about Yousef's grandfather?
options: He saw nothing and knew nothing
He has the same power and knew Yousef's secret
He was angry that Yousef used his power

pages.text: Omar had waited all winter for this trip. His family drove for four hours into the desert north of Riyadh, until the road turned into soft orange sand. They put up two large tents next to a tall dune. Omar's father made a fire while his mother prepared tea with mint.

That night, Grandfather sat with Omar and his sister Lina under a sky full of stars. 'In the past, travellers didn't have maps or phones,' he said quietly. He pointed at one bright star that didn't seem to move. 'That is the North Star. It always shows you the way north, so if you ever get lost, look for it.'

The next afternoon, Omar noticed some small footprints near the tents. 'A fennec fox!' Lina whispered, because she had read about these tiny desert foxes with huge ears. The children followed the tracks over one dune, then another, then another. They were so excited that they didn't notice the sun was going down.

Suddenly, the sky turned purple, and then dark grey. Omar looked around, but every dune looked exactly the same. 'Which way is the camp?' he asked, and his voice was shaking. Lina took out her phone, but there was no signal, and the battery was almost empty.

'Don't panic,' Lina said, although her heart was beating fast. 'Think. When we left, the setting sun was on our left, wasn't it?' Omar nodded slowly. 'Then we were walking north,' she explained. 'So to go back, we need to walk south, with the North Star behind us.'

They waited a few minutes while the stars appeared one by one. Then Omar saw it: the bright, still star that Grandfather had shown them. 'There it is!' he shouted. They turned their backs to it and started walking, holding hands so they wouldn't lose each other in the dark.

The sand was cold now, and the walk felt much longer than before. After about half an hour, Lina stopped. Far away, there was a small orange light flickering between two dunes. 'It's our fire!' Omar cried, and they ran down the dune as fast as they could.

Their parents hugged them tightly, and their mother couldn't stop thanking God. Grandfather looked serious at first, but then he smiled. 'You were careless to walk so far,' he said, 'but you were clever to remember the stars.' Later, as they drank warm milk by the fire, a small fox with enormous ears watched them quietly from the top of the dune.

questions.q: Where did the family put up their tents?
Why did Omar and Lina walk away from the camp?
options: To find a better place for the tents
To follow the tracks of a fennec fox

questions.q: In page 7, the word 'flickering' describes a light that…
options: moves and shines on and off, like a small fire

questions.q: Why did the children walk with the North Star behind them?
options: Because the camp was to the south
Because the star was too bright to look at

questions.q: How did Grandfather probably feel at the end of the story?
options: Worried at first, but proud of them

stories.title: The Voice in the Wooden Box

pages.text: When Dad said that Grandpa Saleh was coming to live with us in Riyadh, I smiled politely. Inside, I was not smiling at all. Grandpa was going to sleep in my room, and I was going to sleep on a mattress in my little brother's room. My brother Omar is seven, and he talks in his sleep.

Grandpa arrived on a hot Thursday with one suitcase and a wooden box. He didn't say much at dinner, and he went to bed early. I was annoyed because my games console was still in his room. "You can come in whenever you want, Yousef," he told me, but I felt like a guest in my own house.

One evening, I knocked on the door to get my phone charger. Grandpa was sitting on the bed, holding an old cassette tape and looking very sad. "This is the only recording of my father's voice," he explained. "He's telling the story of the night he got lost in the desert, but my player broke and now the tape is tangled."

I had never seen a real cassette before, only in old films. But I'm good at fixing things, so I said, "Let me try, Grandpa." He hesitated, then nodded. Very carefully, I put a pencil into one of the holes and turned it slowly until the brown tape was wound back inside. It took nearly an hour, and my hands were shaking by the end.

Fixing the tape wasn't enough, because we needed something to play it on. The next morning, I went with Grandpa to the old market in Al-Batha. We searched shop after shop, and the sellers laughed kindly when we asked for a cassette player. Finally, an old man found one at the back of his shop, covered in dust. "It still works," he promised with a wink, "just like your grandfather."

That night, we sat together on the bed and pressed play. At first there was only a soft hiss, and then a deep, warm voice filled the room. My great-grandfather was describing the stars he had followed to find his way home. Grandpa closed his eyes and smiled, and I suddenly noticed that the voice sounded exactly like Dad's.

Then I had an idea. If the cassette broke again, the story would be lost forever, so I recorded it on my laptop and saved it in three different places. I also sent a copy to everyone in the family. When Grandpa saw the file on my phone, he didn't say anything. He just put his hand on my shoulder, and that was enough.

On Friday, the whole family gathered at our house for lunch, and we played the recording for my uncles, aunts and cousins. Even Omar was quiet for once. Afterwards, Grandpa began telling his own stories, and this time I recorded every word. I still sleep on a mattress next to my brother, but I don't mind anymore, because some things are far more important than having your own room.

questions.q: Why was Yousef unhappy at the start of the story?
options: He had to give his room to Grandpa.
He didn't like living in Riyadh.
His brother broke his games console.

questions.q: What did Yousef use to fix the tangled tape?
In the story, what does "hesitated" mean?
Why did Yousef save the recording in three different places?
options: So he could sell copies at the market
Because the laptop was very old
So the story would never be lost

questions.q: What can we understand about Grandpa when he puts his hand on Yousef's shoulder without speaking?
options: He is too tired to talk.
He is deeply grateful and proud of Yousef.
He wants Yousef to leave the room.

pages.text: Omar had flown his drone every day since Eid, when his uncle gave it to him as a present. It had a special camera that could see heat, even in the dark. "It's the best thing I've ever owned," he told his sister Layla as they drove to their grandfather's farm near AlUla. Layla laughed. "You say that about every new gadget."

Grandfather did not trust machines very much. He preferred his old radio, his notebook and the stars. "Your phone tells you everything," he said to Omar at dinner, "but does it teach you to think?" Omar smiled politely, but he was sure that technology could solve almost any problem.

The next afternoon, the sky turned orange and a strong wind began to blow. "Sandstorm!" Grandmother called. Everyone hurried inside, but then Layla noticed that their little cousin Sami was missing. His favourite baby camel had escaped, and Sami had run after it into the desert.

Omar's father tried to call for help, but there was no signal. Then the electricity went off, and the house became dark and silent. "My drone!" Omar shouted. "If I fly it above the storm, the heat camera might find Sami." But when he checked the screen, the battery was only at fifteen percent.

"Fifteen percent won't last long," Layla said. "We need to know where to look first." Grandfather opened his notebook and turned the old pages carefully. "When camels are frightened, they always walk towards the old well," he explained. "It is three kilometres east, near the tall rocks."

The storm was getting weaker when Omar sent the drone east. Everyone crowded around the small screen, holding their breath. After two minutes, two warm shapes appeared beside the rocks, one big and one small. "It's Sami and the camel!" Layla cried. Then the screen went black.

Father and Grandfather drove slowly through the dust in the old truck, following Grandfather's directions. Half an hour later, they returned with Sami, who was sandy and tired but safe. The baby camel walked happily behind the truck as if nothing had happened. They even brought back the drone, which had landed softly in the sand. Grandmother hugged Sami tightly and made everyone sweet tea.

Later, Omar sat with his grandfather under the clear night sky. "Your drone found him," Grandfather said, "but my notebook told it where to go." Omar grinned. "So we needed both, the old and the new." Grandfather nodded, then smiled shyly. "Tomorrow, will you teach me how to fly that thing?"

questions.q: What was special about Omar's drone?
options: It could fly without a battery
Its camera could see heat in the dark

questions.q: Why did Sami go into the desert?
options: He wanted to fly the drone
He was looking for the old well
He ran after his baby camel

questions.q: Why couldn't Omar's father call for help?
In the story, what does "frightened" mean?
What can we guess about Grandfather at the end of the story?
options: He still thinks technology is useless
He is angry that Omar lost the drone
He now sees that new technology can be useful too
